beginner: Growth slowed to 2.2% after hitting 4.3% last quarter, meaning the AI-fueled sprint is cooling down.
The economy is still expanding, but half as fast as it was a few months ago, so the Fed's holding rates steady to avoid strangling growth further.
Watch whether consumer spending stays strong through Q2, because if households pull back, 2.2% could drop to 1% by year-end.
moderate: The deceleration from 4.3% to 2.2% reflects the fading tailwind of AI capex and inventory builds that powered early 2025.
Compared to the pre-pandemic trend of 2.1%, today's 2.2% barely clears the bar, leaving no room for recession without triggering policy reversals.
Labor market weakness is the leading edge of this slowdown, so if job losses accelerate past the current pace, GDP revisions could fall another 30 basis points by summer.
expert: Q1 2026 prints 2.2% annualized after Q3 2025's 4.3%, signaling fade in both AI investment pull-forward and excess demand from fiscal transfers.
Real rate of 0.95% (3.25% policy minus 2.3% CPI) is restrictive relative to neutral, yet headline inflation risks keep the Fed on hold through December per forward guidance.
Watch ISM manufacturing PMI and jobless claims: if initial claims breach 350k sustainably, the Fed will cut 75bps by Q4 2026, supporting GDP back to 2.8%.

beginner: Inflation is 2.3% right now, which sounds good, but the OECD says it will jump to 4.2% later in 2026, so the Fed's not celebrating yet.
The Fed expected inflation to stay low, but the OECD sees higher pressure building, which means the central bank may have to raise rates again instead of cutting them.
If 4.2% becomes real, that erases 1.9 points of buying power from paychecks, so watch grocery and energy prices closely over the next two quarters.
moderate: CPI at 2.3% is below the Fed's 2.5% warning line, but the OECD's 4.2% forecast for late 2026 contrasts sharply with Fed staff projections, signaling a credibility gap on sticky services inflation.
Core inflation (ex-food and energy) has proved slower to fall than in prior cycles, and shelter costs remain elevated at 4.8%, anchoring expectations above the Fed's comfort zone.
The fiscal deficit at 6.9% of GDP continues to pump demand into the economy, pushing against the Fed's disinflation narrative and raising the odds of an inflation re-acceleration by Q3.
expert: Headline CPI at 2.3% masks core CPI running 3.1%, with shelter contributing 65bps of that and goods deflation providing only partial offset.

OECD's 4.2% call for 2026 reflects their view that the 2023-2025 disinflation cycle ends here, while the Fed's December hold stance betrays concern that rate cuts would re-ignite demand in a 6.9% deficit environment.

Monitor breakeven inflation rates at the 10Y: they've held 2.35% despite core CPI stickiness, suggesting markets don't yet believe the OECD, but a shift above 2.5% would force the Fed to extend hold guidance into 2027.

beginner: Joblessness is at 4.2%, which is still low by historical standards, but it's been creeping up as companies slow hiring.
The job market is weakening while the Fed holds rates steady, so if unemployment keeps rising, the Fed will have to cut rates to prevent a recession.
Watch March and April payroll reports, because if job growth falls below 100k per month, unemployment could hit 4.8% by summer and force policy action.
moderate: At 4.2%, unemployment remains below the Fed's estimated natural rate of 4.3%, but the upward drift from 3.7% last summer signals labor demand is tightening faster than expected.

The current rate is still below the 4.5-4.7% zone that typically precedes recessions, but the combination of slowing GDP growth and elevated rates creates a narrowing window before jobless claims spike.

Wage growth, currently running 3.8% year-over-year, will decelerate if unemployment drifts above 4.5%, which would take inflation pressure off but also confirm the Fed's timing on a pivot is too late.
expert: Unemployment at 4.2% (up from 3.7% in Q2 2025) coincides with initial jobless claims averaging 245k, near the cycle-low but with an upward bias suggesting the labor market is normalizing.
Fed funds futures imply no cuts until December, yet jobless claims need to reach 350k before the committee will move, creating a lag risk where unemployment overshoots to 5.1% before policy responds.
Track the employment cost index (currently 3.9% YoY): if it falls below 3.2% while unemployment rises above 4.5%, the Fed will cut 50bps in December and an additional 75bps across 2027.

beginner: The US government is spending 6.9% more than it collects in taxes each year, a massive gap that forces it to borrow heavily and crowd out private investment.
This deficit is the highest outside of crisis years, which means the Treasury is issuing bonds constantly, pushing up interest rates for mortgages and car loans for regular people.
If the deficit stays above 6%, the government's interest payments could hit 4% of GDP by 2030, eating up money that could go to schools, infrastructure, or tax cuts.
moderate: At 6.9% of GDP, the deficit is bloated relative to the 3% long-term average and even worse than the 5.8% posted in 2021 during peak stimulus.
The 10Y yield at 4.3% reflects foreign and domestic investors demanding compensation for financing this gap, crowding out business capex and keeping mortgage rates elevated.

Tax revenue as a share of GDP has fallen to 17.2% (pre-pandemic was 17.6%), while spending remains elevated at 24.1%, leaving little room to close the gap without recession-level tax hikes or cuts to entitlements.
expert: At 6.9% of GDP, the structural deficit (deficit adjusted for the business cycle) sits at 5.4%, implying even full employment won't close this gap without policy changes.

Treasury borrowing needs of 1.8 trillion dollars for fiscal 2026 force the Fed to maintain restrictive rates longer, keeping real rates at 0.95%, which depresses capex and explains why GDP growth faded from 4.3% to 2.2%.

If Congress doesn't address entitlements or revenues, interest payments alone will force a fiscal crisis by 2030 when they reach 3.5% of GDP, triggering either a sharp tightening or currency instability that breaks the 10Y yield higher to 5.5%.

beginner: The US buys 3.7% more stuff from other countries than it sells to them, a trade gap that means Americans are living beyond their means.
This deficit is funded by foreign investors buying US bonds and stocks, which works as long as the dollar stays strong and returns stay high.
If foreign investors lose confidence, they'll sell dollars, the currency will weaken, and imported goods (phones, cars, clothes) will become more expensive for US consumers.
moderate: The current account deficit of 3.7% is running near the post-2008 average of 3.1%, reflecting structural oversaving abroad and the dollar's reserve status, which lets the US borrow cheaply.
Goods trade is in deficit by 4.8% of GDP while services show a small surplus of 1.1%, meaning America's manufacturing base continues to shrink relative to imports from Asia and Mexico.

The dollar strength at 100.1 DXY buys time by making US assets attractive, but if global growth accelerates or the Fed cuts rates, foreign buying could dry up, forcing the current account to adjust via a weaker dollar or recession.
expert: Current account deficit of 3.7% of GDP (830 billion dollars annualized) is offset by 2.1% of GDP in net inflows to the capital account, leaving a financing gap of 1.6% of GDP that must come from reserve drawdown or currency depreciation.

Goods deficit is 710 billion dollars (3.1% of GDP) while services surplus is only 240 billion dollars (1.1%), so the US cannot grow out of this imbalance without either collapsing goods imports via recession or achieving a structural shift in global supply chains.

If dollar weakness accelerates (DXY falls below 95 by Q4 2026), imported inflation will spike 80-100bps, forcing the Fed to hold rates higher for longer and depressing GDP growth to 1.2% by 2027, which would then reverse the current account via import compression.

beginner: The Federal Reserve is holding interest rates at 3.25%, meaning it's not cutting or raising for now while it waits to see if inflation really stays low.
At 3.25%, borrowing is still expensive for businesses and homebuyers, which slows down investment and hiring, but the Fed wants to avoid cutting too early and reigniting inflation.
If unemployment keeps rising or inflation falls faster than expected, the Fed will start cutting rates in late 2026, which would lower mortgage rates and car loans for everyone.
moderate: The Fed's hold at 3.25% is restrictive relative to nominal GDP growth of 5.1%, leaving a negative real rate of only 0.95%, which should be easing financial conditions but isn't because of fiscal drag and credit supply constraints.

The committee signaled no cuts until December, but that guidance assumes inflation stays above 2.5% and unemployment stays below 4.5%, two conditions that are already at risk given the 2.2% GDP growth and 4.2% joblessness.

Market pricing now implies 50bps of cuts by end-2026 and another 75bps in 2027, which would take the policy rate to 2%, compressing real rates to minus 0.3% and fueling a asset reflation if inflation proves sticky.
expert: Funds rate at 3.25% is 130bps above the market-implied terminal rate of 1.95%, creating an inverted yield curve (+69bps) that historically precedes recession within 6-12 months.

Fed funds futures show zero probability of a cut before December, 40% chance of a 25bps cut in December, and full pricing for 75bps of cuts in 2027, implying the committee will move only after unemployment breaches 4.8% or core CPI falls below 2.8%.

Watch the May and June FOMC statements: if the Fed removes language about 'further tightening,' that signals a June cut is back in play, which would spike equities +4% and bonds +2% immediately, as markets currently price December-or-nothing.

beginner: US stocks are down 4.1% so far this year, meaning investors have lost money if they bought at the start of 2026.
The decline reflects worry that the Fed will keep rates high longer than expected while company earnings growth slows down.

Watch earnings season in April and May, because if companies report slower profit growth, stocks could fall another 5-8%, but if earnings surprise to the upside, we could bounce back to flat or positive.
moderate: The YTD decline of 4.1% is driven by rotation out of mega-cap AI stocks (down 8% YTD) and into small-cap value (+2% YTD), signaling investors are repricing growth assumptions as real rates remain elevated at 0.95%.

The 10Y yield at 4.30% makes bonds more competitive with equities, and the dividend yield on the S&P 500 at 1.8% is still half the 10Y, creating a 250bps equity risk premium that's compressed relative to the pre-2020 average of 400bps.

Earnings growth estimates for 2026 have fallen from 12% to 7% over the past two months, and if Q1 results disappoint, consensus could drop to 5%, which would justify a further 8-10% downside in the index.
expert: S&P 500 YTD at -4.1% (down to 5,840 from 6,085) reflects a 4.2% multiple compression (from 21.8x to 20.9x forward earnings) as the Fed's December hold extends the tightening cycle.

Earnings per share growth of 6% YoY (below long-term 8% trend) combined with a 70bps rise in the 10Y yield to 4.30% has justified the multiple compression, but if the Fed cuts 50bps by December, the forward PE could re-expand to 22.5x and lift the index to 6,400.

Monitor the Russell 2000 (small-cap): currently up 3% YTD vs. the S&P's -4.1%, it acts as a canary for Fed cut expectations, so if small-caps fall back below January levels, it signals the market is pricing a recession before rate cuts arrive.

beginner: The 10-year bond yield is 4.30%, which means the government pays 4.30% interest on long-term loans, and mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs track this number closely.
When yields are this high, it gets expensive for people to buy homes and companies to expand, which slows economic growth.
If the Fed starts cutting rates in December, the 10Y should fall toward 3.8%, making borrowing cheaper, but if inflation surprises higher (as the OECD predicts), yields could climb to 4.8% instead.
moderate: The 4.30% yield reflects a 2.0% term premium above the Fed funds rate of 3.25%, which is elevated relative to the long-term average of 80bps, signaling investors demand compensation for duration risk and fiscal concerns.

Compared to March 2024 when the 10Y hit 4.29%, today's level suggests the market has bought the Fed's December hold narrative, but the OECD's 4.2% inflation call for late 2026 is pushing back against consensus expectations.

If breakeven inflation rates (currently 2.35%) stay above 2.5%, real yields stay elevated above 1.8%, which keeps the yield from falling even if the Fed cuts 50bps, leaving mortgage rates stuck near 7.2%.
expert: The 10Y at 430bps is 15bps above December's close of 415bps, driven by a 4bps rise in real yields (from 176bps to 180bps) and 11bps of inflation premium expansion as the OECD's 4.2% forecast creates uncertainty.

The 2-10Y spread is inverted at minus 69bps, and history shows this persists for an average of 18 months before yield curve control or recession forces normalization, which would allow the 10Y to fall to 3.20% if recession lands by late 2026.

If the OECD's inflation call proves right and CPI hits 4.2% in Q3 2026, real yields will need to stay above 2.2% (requiring a 6.4% nominal yield) unless the Fed pre-emptively cuts, which markets currently assess at 25% probability by June.

beginner: The yield curve is inverted by 69 basis points, which means short-term interest rates are higher than long-term rates, a sign that investors expect economic trouble ahead.
An inverted curve has predicted most recessions in US history, so financial markets and companies are nervous about 2026.
Watch whether the curve un-inverts (the 2-year yield drops below the 10-year) over the next two quarters, because a return to normal slopes would signal the market thinks a recession is off.
moderate: The inversion of 69bps (with 2Y at 4.99% and 10Y at 4.30%) is steep by recent standards, deeper than the 40bps inversion last July and similar to the 80bps of early 2023 that preceded last year's regional bank crisis.
Historically, the curve un-inverts 6-12 months before recession, so the current inversion suggests trouble between Q2 and Q4 2026 unless the Fed cuts 50bps+ before then.

If the Fed doesn't cut by June and unemployment stays below 4.5%, the curve could steepen only via further 10Y decline (to 3.8%), which requires a major drop in inflation expectations or a recession signal that actually causes damage.
expert: The 2-10Y inversion of 69bps sits near the Q1 2023 peak of 80bps and well beyond the 40bps needed to trigger forward guidance markets price for December cuts at only 40% probability.

Curve steepeners (buying the 10Y, selling the 2Y) have become consensus trades, but flows have only pushed the 10Y down 5bps and the 2Y up 8bps over the past month, signaling limited room for curve un-inversion without an actual Fed cut or major risk-off event.

If the Fed extends its hold into June (now 60% priced), the curve will likely steepen via 10Y compression to 4.0% and 2Y fall to 4.5%, pricing a September cut, which would confirm the recession case and trigger 15% equity downside to 5,000 on the S&P 500.

beginner: The dollar is trading at 100.1 on the DXY index, which measures it against other major currencies, meaning the dollar is strong and getting stronger.
A strong dollar is good news for American tourists and investors buying foreign assets, but bad news for US exporters because their products become more expensive for foreigners to buy.
If the dollar stays strong, the US current account deficit of 3.7% will keep growing, but if the Fed starts cutting rates later this year, the dollar could weaken to 95-97 by year-end.
moderate: The DXY at 100.1 is at the highest level since March 2020, driven by real rate differentials (US real yields at 1.8% versus eurozone at 1.1%) and safe-haven flows as growth slows.
US exports have declined 2.3% YoY in volume terms, and the dollar's strength explains roughly 60% of that drag, with the remaining 40% from weakening global demand.

If the Fed cuts 50bps by December while the ECB waits, the DXY could fall to 96-98, which would provide a 2-3% tailwind to US multinational earnings and partially offset the revenue headwind from the 6.9% budget deficit.
expert: DXY at 100.1 reflects a 6% appreciation since May 2024 (from 94.5), driven by 140bps of real rate premium over the eurozone and BoE, which has created a 30bps net capital inflow to US assets despite an inverted yield curve.

Real effective exchange rate (REER) at 107.3 is 15% above the 2019 average, compressing ex-energy exports to 9.2% of GDP (lowest since 2009) and widening the goods deficit to 3.1% of GDP, which is unsustainable without a Fed cut cycle.

Monitor EUR/USD: currently 1.087, it needs to break above 1.12 to trigger Fed cut frontloading, which happens only if US CPI falls below 2.0% or unemployment exceeds 4.8% before June, scenarios we assess at 35% combined probability.

beginner: When measured in dollars, US stocks are down 3.12% so far this year, slightly better than the headline 4.1% because the strong dollar adds a small cushion for international investors.
For someone holding dollars, stocks have lost more ground (4.1%) than for someone holding euros or other currencies who gets a 1% benefit from dollar appreciation.
This matters because it shows the strong dollar is a headwind for US equity valuations, and if the Fed cuts and the dollar weakens, stocks could bounce harder than the headline numbers suggest.
moderate: The 3.12% USD-adjusted loss versus the 4.1% headline loss means the DXY's 6% appreciation since May 2024 has provided a 98bps tailwind to USD-denominated returns, masking the full extent of valuation compression.

For foreign investors, the 3.12% loss in USD terms translates to a 4.1% loss in local currency, making US stocks less attractive relative to emerging markets (up 5.2% YTD in USD), creating potential for capital flows to reverse if the Fed pivots.

If the DXY falls 5% by December (to 95 from 100.1), that 98bps headwind becomes a 98bps tailwind, which alone would support 110bps of additional index return and reduce the YTD loss to 2.0% even if valuations don't expand.
expert: The gap between headline (-4.1%) and USD-adjusted (-3.12%) returns of 98bps reflects the DXY's 6% strength since May 2024, which has compressed reported earnings of overseas subsidiaries by roughly 100bps YoY.

S&P 500 earnings have 36% exposure to overseas revenues, so a further 3% dollar appreciation would knock 110bps off reported EPS growth, taking 2026 consensus from 7% to 5.9%, which justifies current 20.9x forward PE.

If the Fed cuts 50bps by December and the DXY falls to 96-98, the 200-300bps of currency tailwind would offset a 30% earnings miss and still support a 6-8% rally in the index to 6,200, creating asymmetry favoring tacticals into the summer swoon.

beginner: The Fed is stuck. Inflation keeps climbing faster than expected while the job market weakens, so the central bank can't cut rates until December at the earliest.
The economy is still firing on all cylinders thanks to AI spending and consumers who keep buying, but that strength is making the inflation problem worse.
The disconnect between what the Fed predicted (2.3% inflation) and what's actually happening (4.2% according to the OECD) means rate cuts are further away than markets hoped.
moderate: The Fed faces an unusual bind: Q3 GDP clocked 4.3-4.4% annualized growth driven by AI capital spending, yet the OECD expects 4.2% inflation versus the Fed's 2.3% forecast, forcing the central bank to hold rates steady through December despite a weakening labor market.

Consumer spending remains resilient even as unemployment ticks up to 4.4%, suggesting households are spending down savings or confidence hasn't cracked yet, but this buoyancy is exactly what keeps inflation sticky.

The Fed's December hold through to the next move depends on whether inflation prints start tracking closer to 2.3% or stay elevated near 4%, which would validate the OECD's gloomier view and delay relief for borrowers.
expert: CPI at 2.41% in February sits well above the Fed's 2% target, and with OECD forecasting 4.2% inflation for the year (versus the Fed's 2.3%), the central bank anchors policy at 3.64% with no cuts priced until December, implying a 275 basis point policy rate in real terms.

Real GDP growth at 4.3-4.4% annualized in Q3 2025 powered by AI and capex spending creates upside risks to the OECD inflation forecast if labor productivity gains lag capex returns, and unemployment at 4.4% is creeping toward the 4.2% full-year consensus.

Watch whether March and April CPI prints narrow the gap between Fed expectations and OECD forecasts, because sustained inflation above 3.5% through Q2 would lock in higher terminal rates than the 3.25% full-year consensus and compress growth expectations from 2.2% toward 1.8%.

fxRegime.label: Free Float
fxRegime.beginner: The US dollar floats freely - its value is set by supply and demand in global markets. As the world's reserve currency, the dollar is the benchmark against which most other currencies are measured. The DXY index shown here is not a single exchange rate - it measures the dollar's strength against a basket of 6 major currencies (euro, yen, pound, Canadian dollar, Swedish krona, Swiss franc). A DXY of 104 means the dollar is 4% stronger than the basket's baseline value of 100.
fxRegime.moderate: Free float. The dollar's value is market-determined with no intervention target. The Fed does not have an exchange rate mandate, though dollar strength has indirect policy implications via financial conditions and import prices. The DXY index measures USD against a basket of 6 major currencies.
fxRegime.expert: Pure free float with no FX intervention since the Plaza/Louvre era. The dollar operates as the global numeraire and primary reserve/invoicing currency (~58% of allocated reserves per IMF COFER). Treasury's Exchange Stabilization Fund exists but is dormant. Dollar valuation is a function of relative growth differentials, rate spreads, and safe-haven flows - the "dollar smile" framework applies.

GDP Growth.beginner: The US economy grew solidly in 2025 fuelled by consumer spending and a strong stock market, but growth is expected to slow in 2026 as tariffs raise costs and hiring weakens.
GDP Growth.moderate: US GDP growth is forecast at 2.6% for 2026 (above consensus), driven by OBBBA tax cuts and easier financial conditions, but tariff drag and a deteriorating labour market (unemployment trending toward 4.4%) pose meaningful downside risk.
GDP Growth.expert: Goldman forecasts US real GDP at 2.6% for 2026, outperforming consensus by 0.6pp on the strength of the OBBBA fiscal impulse and reduced tariff drag post-SCOTUS IEEPA ruling; the Iran oil shock introduces a stagflationary supply-side headwind that could compress the growth rate by 0.3-0.5pp if Brent stays above $90 through Q2.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: US prices rose 2.4% in January compared to a year earlier, still above the Fed's 2% target, and the jump in oil prices from the Middle East conflict could push inflation higher again in the coming months.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: US CPI was 2.4% in January (ex-shutdown distortions ~2.7%), with tariff passthrough expected to add 0.3pp in H1 2026; the Iran energy shock could add a further 0.5-1.0pp, raising the risk that CPI reaches 3%+ by mid-year, complicating Fed rate-cut planning significantly.
Inflation (CPI).expert: US PCE inflation (the Fed's preferred gauge) ran at approximately 2.6% entering 2026; tariff-driven goods CPI uplift (+1.3-1.4% on imported durables in 2025) is now being compounded by an energy-driven CPI spike, and Goldman estimates the Iran shock alone could add 0.5pp to US CPI within 6 weeks if crude stays at current levels, a scenario the FOMC did not price in its December dot plot.

Unemployment.beginner: About 130,000 new jobs were created in January, fewer than expected, and the unemployment rate has risen to 4.4%, a sign the job market is cooling as businesses become more cautious about hiring.
Unemployment.moderate: January payrolls of 130,000 (private +172k, federal -42k) masked underlying weakness: ex-healthcare, private sector job creation was just 6,500; the unemployment rate has drifted to 4.4%, and IT employment fell 12,000, consistent with AI-driven displacement beginning to register in headline data.
Unemployment.expert: The K-shaped US labour market (healthcare/social assistance absorbing +123,500 jobs while IT shed 12,000 and manufacturing and wholesale contracted) is consistent with AI-driven productivity reallocation depressing labour demand in white-collar sectors; the FOMC's dual-mandate tension is now acute as unemployment trends higher even as tariff-and-energy-driven inflation runs above target.

Budget Deficit.beginner: The US government is borrowing heavily, with a deficit of around 6% of GDP, meaning the government spends much more than it collects in taxes, and tariff revenues of about $194 billion in 2025 only partially offset the gap.
Budget Deficit.moderate: The US fiscal deficit is running near 6% of GDP, sustained by structural entitlement spending and the OBBBA tax cut impulse; tariff revenues ($194bn above 2022-24 average in 2025) partially offset cost, but the Section 122 tariff (replacing struck-down IEEPA tariffs) adds only ~$22.3bn annually, leaving a structurally wide deficit.
Budget Deficit.expert: Post-SCOTUS IEEPA ruling (Feb 20), the US tariff revenue base shifted to Section 232 + Section 122 (temporary 10%) + pre-existing Section 301 China tariffs; TPC estimates total tariff revenue of $194bn in 2026, but the OBBBA's multi-trillion dollar cost and rising debt service (10-year Treasury ~4.2%) are widening the structural primary deficit, constraining the Fed's ability to QE in a crisis without fiscal dominance concerns.

Current Account.beginner: The US buys far more from the rest of the world than it sells, creating a large trade deficit that tariffs were supposed to reduce, but the deficit has not meaningfully narrowed despite record tariff revenues.
Current Account.moderate: The US current account deficit has remained stubbornly wide despite tariff-driven import compression; the Tax Foundation estimates tariffs have 'not meaningfully altered the trade deficit' as dollar strength offsets competitiveness gains; the Iran oil shock could temporarily widen the energy trade deficit before domestic production responds.
Current Account.expert: The persistence of the US current account deficit despite historically high tariff rates confirms the Lerner symmetry theorem in practice: tariffs on imports are offset by equivalent tariffs on exports via currency adjustment and income effects; the structural determinant is the gap between domestic saving and investment, a gap that OBBBA fiscal expansion is actively widening by reducing national saving.

Policy Rate.beginner: The Federal Reserve has kept interest rates at 4.25-4.5%, pausing its rate cuts from last year, as it waits to see whether prices keep falling toward its 2% target, which is now more uncertain because of the oil price spike.
Policy Rate.moderate: The FOMC has been on hold at 4.25-4.5% since late 2025; markets that had priced June cuts before the Iran shock have now pushed the first cut expectation to July-September; FOMC members face a classic stagflation dilemma and NY Fed's Williams has explicitly said tariff-driven inflation has 'temporarily stalled' progress toward the 2% target.
Policy Rate.expert: The FOMC's reaction function is now constrained on multiple dimensions: the dual tariff-and-energy supply shock argues against rate cuts (inflation upside risk), while a cooling labour market and deteriorating business confidence argue for easing; the December dot plot (two cuts in 2026) is now likely inoperative, and any shift toward the 'stagflation hold' scenario would materially re-price the front end of the US rates curve with knock-on effects on EM capital flows and USD strength.

beginner: Canada's economy grew just 1.7% last year, which is the slowest pace in the G7 and signals that households and businesses are pulling back spending.
Growth this weak means the Bank of Canada has room to cut rates further without worrying about overheating, but it also means job creation will struggle to keep up with population growth.
Watch whether the USMCA renegotiation produces tariffs on Canadian goods, because even a 10% US tariff on autos would shave 0.3 to 0.5 percentage points off annual growth.
moderate: At 1.7%, Canada's growth trails the US (2.3%) and sits well below its 2.1% pre-pandemic trend, reflecting weak consumer confidence and business investment freezes tied to trade uncertainty.

The Bank of Canada cut rates to 2.25% precisely because growth stalled, and the central bank signaled three more cuts this year if inflation stays anchored, which would ease debt service costs for households carrying record leverage.
Tariff headwinds from USMCA renegotiation could suppress growth by 40 to 60 basis points if Trump follows through, pushing the Bank of Canada toward 1.5% or lower by year-end.
expert: Q4 2025 real GDP printed at 1.7% annualized, a deceleration from 2.1% in Q3, driven by collapsing business investment (down 8% YoY) and consumption growth cut to 0.9%, the weakest since 2020.

The output gap has swung negative (roughly 0.8 to 1.2% slack), giving the Bank of Canada cover for a 100+ basis point rate cut cycle through 2026, with June and September easing moves now priced in at 75% probability.

Model-based scenarios suggest tariffs at 15% to 25% applied to 40% to 60% of Canadian exports would trim 2026 growth by 0.4 to 0.8 percentage points; watch April trade data for signs of front-loading or diversion.

beginner: Canada's inflation rate sits at 2%, right in the Bank of Canada's target zone, so price pressures have cooled dramatically from the 5.5% peak in 2022.
With inflation under control, the central bank can focus on supporting jobs instead of fighting runaway prices, which is why rate cuts are coming this year.
Monitor energy prices and the Canadian dollar's weakness against the US dollar, because a weaker loonie (now at 0.72 USD) makes imports more expensive and could nudge inflation back up toward 2.5%.
moderate: Inflation at 2% marks a full return to target after climbing to 5.5% in mid-2022, a journey driven by energy shocks and supply-chain pressures that have since reversed; core inflation sits even lower at 1.8%.

Canada's disinflation outpaced the US (3.2% CPI) because energy price declines hit harder here and wage growth remained more moderate, giving the Bank of Canada more flexibility to ease than the Federal Reserve.

CAD weakness to 0.72 USD creates imported inflation risk if sustained, but trade volume contraction from tariff threats could offset this by reducing import demand and keeping price pressures muted through 2026.
expert: Headline CPI at 2.0% YoY (March 2026 flash) with core PCE at 1.8% signals an undershooting risk; the Bank of Canada's 2% midpoint target is now the ceiling, not the center of expectations.

Energy's drag has faded (gasoline at 105 CAD cents/liter, flat YoY), so disinflation drivers have shifted to core goods and services softness tied to negative output gap and wage moderation (1.8% growth, down from 3.1% in 2022).

CAD depreciation to 0.72 (+5% risk premium embedded in options markets) will put 20 to 30 basis points of upside pressure on inflation in 2H 2026 if sustained, but tariff-driven demand collapse could overwhelm this channel.

beginner: Canada's jobless rate climbed to 6.5%, the highest in three years, signaling that employers have stopped hiring as growth slowed and business confidence deteriorated.
Unemployment this high gives the Bank of Canada strong reason to cut rates aggressively, because lower borrowing costs can encourage companies to hire and expand.
Immigration policy changes and trade tensions will determine whether joblessness keeps rising or starts to fall in the next six months, so watch corporate earnings reports and job postings closely.
moderate: At 6.5%, Canada's unemployment sits 180 basis points above its pre-pandemic low of 4.7%, reflecting persistent weakness in hiring despite the Bank of Canada already cutting rates twice since February.

The labor force participation rate has also sagged to 62.1% from 63.3% pre-pandemic, meaning the jobless rate understates slack; combining unemployment and underemployment, the true slack rate approaches 8%.

Trade uncertainty and tariff risks have frozen business hiring plans, and April employment data will be crucial, because even one more month of 20k+ job losses would validate recession scenarios and guarantee 50 basis point cuts in June.
expert: Unemployment at 6.5% (March 2026) represents a 130 basis point rise from the 5.2% trough in September 2023; job losses accelerated in Q1 2026 with 45k departures in February alone, driven by goods-producing sectors and finance.

The output gap has widened to roughly 1.0 to 1.2% as potential GDP growth (2.1%) outpaces actual output growth (1.7%), and labor market slack is now loose enough to justify 25 to 30 basis points of deflation risk if demand doesn't recover.

April and May employment prints will determine the Bank of Canada's June easing magnitude; if jobs continue falling and unemployment hits 6.8%, a 50 basis point cut is locked in; if stabilization occurs, 25 basis points becomes the mode.

beginner: Canada's government is spending 1.5% more than it takes in every year, which means the country is borrowing to cover the gap and that debt is piling up.

A deficit this size is manageable because interest rates are falling and the economy is not overheating, but if growth stays weak and rates stay elevated, the deficit could grow and squeeze other programs.
Watch whether the government cuts spending or raises taxes in the next budget, because without action, the debt-to-GDP ratio will keep climbing and limit fiscal flexibility during a recession.
moderate: The budget deficit of 1.5% of GDP masks a structural deterioration, because the federal government's operating (primary) deficit is closer to 2.2%, meaning even zero interest payments would leave a gap.

Historically, Canada ran near-balanced budgets before 2020, so current deficits reflect elevated pandemic-era spending levels that the government has been reluctant to unwind, compounded by slowing tax revenue from weak growth.

Debt-to-GDP now sits at 53%, up from 49% in 2020, and rating agencies have signaled that further deterioration above 55% could trigger a credit downgrade; the government will face pressure to implement spending restraint if tariff shocks reduce growth further.
expert: The fiscal deficit at 1.5% of GDP (FY2025-26 estimate, April 2026 fiscal update pending) combines a cyclical component (output gap of 1.0 to 1.2%) and a structural component (primary balance of minus 0.8% of GDP even at potential output).

Debt-to-GDP at 53% is sustainable at current real rates (policy rate 2.25%, expected 2026 real growth 1.2%), but sensitivity to a 200 basis point rate shock would push debt servicing costs from 11% to 15% of revenue by 2028.

Tariff scenarios modeling 15% average rate on 50% of exports could reduce tax revenue by 0.4 to 0.6% of GDP and increase the structural deficit to 1.3 to 1.5%, forcing either spending cuts or a 25 to 50 basis point tax increase by late 2026.

beginner: Canada's current account deficit of 0.5% of GDP means the country imports more than it exports and is relying on foreign investment to cover the shortfall.
This deficit matters because it shows Canada's economy is not fully self-sufficient and depends on attracting overseas capital, which could become riskier if tariffs disrupt trade flows.
If the USMCA renegotiation leads to tariffs, Canadian exports will shrink and the current account deficit could widen to 1% or more, requiring higher interest rates to attract foreign money.
moderate: At 0.5% of GDP, Canada's current account deficit remains modest by historical standards (peaked at 3.4% in 2000), but the composition has shifted toward energy and commodity exports weakness offsetting goods-trade surpluses.

The shortfall reflects strong US import demand and a relatively weak Canadian dollar at 0.72 USD, which paradoxically helps exports but signals capital outflow concerns and lower domestic investment returns.

Tariff risks pose a material threat, because Canada's goods trade surplus with the US (mostly autos, oil, and minerals) stands at 2.5% of GDP, and a 20% auto tariff alone would swing this to deficit and widen the current account deficit by 0.8 to 1.0 percentage points.
expert: Canada's current account deficit at 0.5% of GDP (Q4 2025, updated April 2026) has widened from 0.2% in Q3 2025, driven by a goods trade deficit narrowing (from surplus 2.1% to 1.8% of GDP) and primary income outflows (dividend repatriations) at 2.0% of GDP.

The CAD weakness to 0.72 USD (down 3.2% YTD) reflects this structural deficit, yet capital inflows into Canadian equities and bonds (+3.4% YTD stock returns, 3.29% 10Y yield) remain sufficient to finance the gap at current account pressures of 0.5 to 0.7% of GDP.

Tariff scenarios incorporating 20% auto duties on 60% of Canadian exports to the US would collapse the goods trade surplus by 0.9 to 1.2% of GDP, pushing the current account deficit to 1.4 to 1.7% of GDP and forcing either a 5 to 8 cent CAD depreciation or a 50+ basis point rate premium to re-attract capital.

beginner: The Bank of Canada's interest rate stands at 2.25%, down from 5% just 18 months ago, as the central bank cuts to support growth and jobs.
Lower rates make borrowing cheaper for businesses and homeowners, which should encourage spending and hiring, but they also reduce returns on savings accounts and GICs.
Expect at least two more rate cuts this year because inflation is under control and the economy needs support, but watch out for tariff shocks that could reverse the easing cycle.
moderate: The Bank of Canada has cut rates from 5% to 2.25% over 18 months, a pace of easing faster than the Federal Reserve, because Canadian inflation peaked earlier and the labor market has softened more sharply.

Current market pricing implies three more 25 basis point cuts in June, September, and December 2026, bringing the policy rate to 1.5% by year-end, which would match the neutral rate and signal a fully accommodative stance.

However, tariff announcements could force the Bank to pause or reverse easing if the Canadian dollar depreciates sharply or if imported inflation accelerates, so April GDP and trade data will be critical signposts.
expert: The policy rate at 2.25% (April 2026) is 75 basis points below the estimated neutral rate of 3.0%, positioning monetary policy as clearly accommodative; the neutral rate has fallen from 3.5% pre-pandemic owing to lower trend growth (1.8 to 2.0% vs 2.3%).

Market pricing of three 25bp cuts (June, September, December) reflects consensus for a 1.5% terminal rate by Q4 2026, contingent on inflation staying at 2.0% and unemployment stabilizing above 6.2%; terminal rate risk to downside if tariff shocks exceed 15% average equivalence.

Forward guidance and real rate dynamics matter: a 50 basis point cut at the June meeting (now 40% probability priced in) would signal panic over tariff contagion or a recession scenario; holding at June and cutting in September (60% base case) implies the Bank expects tariff impacts to unfold gradually through Q2 Q3.

beginner: Canada's stock market is up 3.4% so far this year, a modest gain that lags the US market and reflects investor caution about trade risks and economic slowdown.
Weakness in Canadian tech stocks and financial companies (which make up 60% of the index) is dragging down overall returns, while energy and materials stocks are holding up better.

If tariff threats ease or the Bank of Canada cuts rates aggressively, the market could accelerate higher, but any economic recession would likely push stocks down another 10 to 15% from current levels.
moderate: The Canadian stock market's 3.4% YTD return trails the S&P 500's 8.2% gain, with weakness concentrated in financials (down 2% YTD as deposit outflows and margin pressures spread) and technology (up just 4% as cross-border M&A uncertainty deters investment).

Energy stocks are outperforming (up 7% YTD) on stable oil prices, but this is masking internal weakness in bank-dependent sectors like real estate and retail, signaling that rate-cut expectations alone are not driving a broad equity rally.

Tariff-driven recession scenarios are now priced into a 15% to 20% downside case for the TSX, with options market implied volatility at 18.5% (elevated), suggesting institutional investors are hedging duration and cyclical exposure.
expert: The TSX Composite has returned 3.4% YTD (through April 2, 2026) versus a 5.8% gain in the S&P 500, driven by underperformance in financials (Toronto-Dominion down 4.8%, RBC down 1.2%) and tech (Shopify down 7.1%, Constellation down 3.4%) offsetting energy gains (Suncor up 8.2%, Cenovus up 6.5%).

Sector attribution shows a 220 basis point drag from financials (higher deposit costs and margin compression from rapid rate cuts), a 180 basis point drag from tech (cross-border deal uncertainty and US growth fears), and a 90 basis point boost from energy on oil price stability.

Tariff scenarios incorporating 20% auto duties and 15% aggregate equivalence have a 35% probability in options markets (3 month 15% downside put skew), pricing in a potential March to June correction to 21,200 (down 12% from current 24,100), with recovery contingent on Bank of Canada cuts offsetting fiscal headwinds and corporate margin compression running 3.5 to 4.5% on the index.

beginner: Canada's 10-year government bond yield stands at 3.29%, which is the interest rate investors demand to lend to the government for a decade.
This yield has fallen from 4.5% a year ago because the Bank of Canada has signaled interest rate cuts, making bonds more valuable to investors seeking stable returns.
If tariffs shock the economy and push Canada toward recession, yields will fall further (to 2.5% to 2.8%) as investors seek safety, but if inflation re-accelerates, yields could spike above 4%.
moderate: The 10Y yield at 3.29% sits 50 basis points below the US 10Y (3.79%), a spread that reflects both lower Canadian growth expectations and the Bank of Canada's faster easing cycle relative to the Federal Reserve.

Yields have declined 120 basis points from the 4.5% peak in October 2023, matching the decline in policy rate expectations and real growth forecasts, with real yields now embedded at 1.3% (nominal 3.29% minus 2% expected inflation).

Watch the April Bank of Canada inflation report and May employment data, because any miss on inflation or jobs will trigger a rally in yields (down to 3.0 to 3.1%), while tariff surprises could cause yields to spike if they threaten fiscal sustainability.
expert: The Canadian 10Y yield at 3.29% (April 2, 2026) is anchored by an expected easing path of three 25bp cuts (75bp cumulative by Q4 2026) and a real growth forecast of 1.2% for 2026 (down from 1.7% consensus in January), reflecting tariff risk premiums.

Real yields at 1.29% (derived from breakeven inflation of 2.0%) sit 60 basis points above US real yields (0.69%), indicating Canada's higher fiscal deficit (1.5% vs 0.8%) is pricing in a duration premium, with options markets suggesting 15% probability of yields spiking to 3.8% if tariff scenarios exceed base case.

Term premium has compressed to 120 basis points (10Y minus 2Y), a 15bp decline YTD, signaling reduced long-term inflation expectations and increased policy uncertainty; a recession scenario would push the 10Y to 2.4 to 2.7% (100+bp rally), while tariff-driven fiscal deterioration to minus 2.2% would require yields to rise 50 to 80bp to maintain debt service coverage.

beginner: Canada's yield curve (difference between 10-year and 2-year bond yields) is 111 basis points, a steep slope that means the market expects interest rates to stay low for a while before rising later.
A steep curve like this suggests investors are not worried about an imminent recession, but it also reflects the Bank of Canada's rate-cut path keeping short-term yields depressed.
If the curve flattens to 50 basis points or inverts (short-term yields above long-term), that would be a warning sign that a recession is coming and the market expects rapid rate cuts.
moderate: The 111 basis point curve slope is steep by historical standards (average is 65bps), reflecting the Bank of Canada's 75bp of expected cuts through 2026, which are pricing in a decline in the 2Y yield to 1.75% while the 10Y anchors near 3.2%.

This steepness masks recession risks embedded elsewhere in the yield curve, because the 5Y10Y spread (7-8Y forward, which is forward-looking) is only 85 basis points, down from 110bps in January and signaling diminishing long-term growth expectations.

Watch the 2Y5Y spread closely, because if it flattens to 40bp or below, that would signal market doubts about the permanence of rate cuts and suggest economic pressures are building; April and May data will be critical.
expert: The Canadian yield curve at 111bps (10Y2Y spread at 3.29% minus 2.18%) sits at the 75th percentile of historical steepness, driven by a 260bp rally in the 2Y yield (from 4.78% in September 2025) as the Bank of Canada signaled three more 25bp cuts, while the 10Y only declined 120bp.

The curve's steepness is primarily a function of expected easing (75bp cumulative cuts), not economic growth optimism; the 5Y10Y spread at 85bp (well below the 110bp average) indicates moderate long-term growth concerns, with terminal real yields implying 1.2% to 1.5% potential growth by 2031.

Recession probability models derived from yield curve inversion metrics score Canada at 22% to 25% (12 month recession odds) versus 18% to 20% for the US, reflecting tariff vulnerability; if the 2Y5Y spread collapses to 35bp or below, recession odds would reach 35% to 40%, likely triggering a 50bp emergency cut and a 10Y yield crash to 2.8% to 2.9%.

beginner: The Canadian dollar trades at 0.72 US cents, down from 0.75 six months ago, meaning it takes more Canadian dollars to buy US goods and travel costs more for Canadians.
The loonie is falling because investors prefer US assets (higher growth, higher returns) and because tariff fears are making them worried about Canada's economic outlook.
If tariffs hit Canada hard, the currency could fall to 0.68 or 0.70, making imports more expensive and squeezing the purchasing power of Canadian consumers and businesses.
moderate: The CAD at 0.72 USD is 4.2% weaker YTD, reflecting a divergence in monetary policy (Bank of Canada faster easing) and growth expectations (US 2.3% vs Canada 1.7%), with tariff risk premiums now embedded at 1.5 to 2.0 cents of depreciation.

Historically, CAD weakness at 0.72 levels puts pain on debt-laden Canadian companies that have US dollar revenues (autos, materials) and on households carrying US dollar mortgages or borrowing, effectively raising debt service costs by 3 to 4%.

Watch central bank comment on currency stability (April 10 BoC meeting) and April trade data, because if the trade deficit widens or tariffs spike, the CAD could break below 0.70 within weeks, triggering technical selling and a potential move to 0.68.
expert: The CAD/USD pair at 0.7200 (April 2, 2026) has depreciated 4.2% YTD from 0.7515, driven by a 260bp decline in Canadian 2Y yields relative to US 2Y yields (which fell only 140bp) and a 150bp widening of real rate differentials favoring the US (real 2Y yield now 0.65% USD vs minus 0.05% CAD).

Tariff risk premiums have embedded a 100 to 120bp depreciation case in the 3 month CAD put options (16.5% implied volatility, 15 delta puts trading at 0.70 strike), with a 30% probability of a break below 0.70 within 60 days if tariff equivalence exceeds 17% average.

The current account deficit at 0.5% of GDP and falling foreign direct investment inflows (down 15% YoY to CAD 28B in Q4 2025) are creating persistent depreciation pressure; a 25bp central bank rate cut in June combined with tariff shocks at 20% average equivalence would likely drive CAD to 0.68 to 0.69, a move that would increase imported inflation by 20 to 30bp and force a policy rate pivot to 50bp cuts or hold.

beginner: When you convert Canadian stock gains to US dollars, the TSX is up just 2.78% YTD instead of 3.4%, because the Canadian dollar has weakened so much that currency losses are eating into returns.
This shows that investors in the US are not making as much money on Canadian stocks as those who hold them in Canadian dollars, a sign that the currency is creating a headwind.
If the loonie keeps falling, Canadian stocks will underperform even more in US dollar terms, discouraging American investors from buying and pushing the market lower.
moderate: The TSX return of 2.78% in USD terms versus 3.4% CAD terms reflects a 62bp currency drag from CAD depreciation to 0.72 USD, meaning that roughly 18% of the YTD underperformance versus the S&P 500 (5.8% gain) is attributable to FX rather than equity selection.

This currency headwind compounds the secular underperformance of Canadian equities tied to lower growth expectations, higher fiscal deficits, and concentrated sector exposure to rate-sensitive financials and commodities with weakening demand.

Watch whether Bank of Canada cuts rates aggressively (100bp total in 2026 base case) and whether tariff threats materialize, because a weaker loonie coupled with economic recession would create a vicious cycle of currency decline and equity weakness, potentially pushing USD returns to negative 2% to 5%.
expert: The TSX's 3.4% CAD return trails its 2.78% USD return by 62 basis points, reflecting CAD depreciation of 4.2% YTD, with the currency accounting for 62bp of the 300bp underperformance relative to the S&P 500's 5.8% return.

Currency drag is concentrated in sectors with US dollar earnings (materials down 3.5% CAD, down 4.0% USD; industrials up 2.2% CAD, up 1.6% USD), while domestic sectors (financials down 2.8% CAD, down 3.4% USD) show added currency losses, indicating broad-based valuation pressure.

Tariff scenarios with 20% equivalent duties drive a 6% to 8% CAD depreciation to 0.66 to 0.68 level, which would translate to 150 to 180bp of additional currency headwinds on USD returns, potentially pushing the TSX to negative 5% to 7% in USD terms even if CAD index holds flat; long-dated options (December 2026) price this scenario at 25% to 28% probability with USD returns expected at minus 3% to 1% under tariff cases.

beginner: Canada's economy faces an existential trade threat as the Trump administration renegotiates USMCA and threatens to extend US-China restrictions to Canadian exports, which would hammer a country already slowing.
The labor market is already weak with unemployment at 6.74%, so tariff shocks would hit when households have fewer jobs to move into and less income cushion.
Inflation at 1.78% gives the Bank of Canada room to cut rates as a policy buffer, but tariffs would create conflicting pressures by driving prices up while crushing demand.
moderate: USMCA renegotiation talks risk extending US-China trade restrictions into Canadian supply chains, a shock the Bank of Canada cannot offset with rate cuts, especially since unemployment at 6.74% is already 0.24 percentage points above the 6.5% full-year forecast.

Canadian CPI at 1.78% is tracking well below the 2% full-year target, giving policymakers room to ease, but any tariff action would instantly create stagflation conditions (rising prices plus weak demand) that rate cuts alone cannot remedy.

The current account deficit sits at an assumed negative level per forecasts, meaning Canada needs healthy trade flows to sustain currency stability, so exclusion from US supply chains would weaken both growth and the loonie simultaneously.
expert: With unemployment at 6.74% and CPI at 1.78%, the Bank of Canada has easing capacity, but tariff extension via USMCA renegotiation would create a policy fork: cut rates and watch the currency depreciate, or hold and let demand collapse further.

If Trump administration tariffs extend to Canada as feared, the transmission mechanism runs through export-dependent sectors (autos, energy) where Canadian firms face dual shocks (margin compression plus lower volumes), and a -1.5% fiscal deficit already limits Ottawa's countercyclical firepower.

Watch whether USMCA text emerges before Q2 earnings season, because visibility on tariff scope will determine whether growth forecasts of 1.7% hold or slide toward 0.5-1.0%, with currency implications for import price passthrough that would offset the disinflationary CPI print.

fxRegime.label: Free Float
fxRegime.beginner: The Canadian dollar floats freely. The Bank of Canada doesn't try to fix its value, but the currency tends to move with oil prices since Canada is a major oil exporter. CAD/USD shows how many US dollars one Canadian dollar buys. At 0.74, one Canadian dollar buys 74 US cents - or flipped, you give up about 1.35 Canadian dollars to buy one US dollar.
fxRegime.moderate: Free float since 1970. The Bank of Canada has not intervened since 1998. CAD is classified as a commodity currency given Canada's oil export dependency - crude oil prices explain ~60% of CAD variance. The BoC monitors FX as a transmission channel but doesn't target a level.
fxRegime.expert: Free float; last intervention Sept 1998. CAD behaves as a petrocurrency - crude WTI correlation ~0.6 over rolling 12M. Terms of trade channel dominant. BoC operationally focused on inflation targeting; FX pass-through to CPI estimated at 0.05-0.08 over 4Q. Cross-border portfolio flows and rate differentials vs Fed are the secondary drivers.

GDP Growth.beginner: Canada's economy has been growing slowly, hurt by uncertainty over US trade policy, though the oil price surge from the Iran conflict is providing a welcome boost to the country's large energy sector.
GDP Growth.moderate: Canadian GDP growth is tracking below potential as tariff uncertainty dampens business investment and the labour market softens; the oil price surge is a near-term positive for Alberta's fiscal revenues but Eastern refiners face higher feedstock costs, creating a regional divergence in the economic impact.
GDP Growth.expert: Canada's terms-of-trade improvement from oil above $90 is mechanically positive for GDP (energy sector is ~10% of the economy), but the structural headwind from US tariff uncertainty — which has suppressed non-energy business investment — is not alleviated by the oil shock and may intensify if Trump uses the Iran crisis as leverage in bilateral trade negotiations.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: Canadian inflation had been coming down steadily, giving the Bank of Canada room to cut interest rates, but higher fuel prices from the Iran conflict could push prices up again and slow the rate-cutting cycle.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: Bank of Canada CPI was tracking toward target before the Iran shock; the energy price spike directly affects Canadian consumers through gasoline and home heating costs, and indirectly through transportation costs — but Canada's position as a net oil exporter means terms-of-trade effects partially insulate the macro from pure imported inflation.
Inflation (CPI).expert: Canada's inflation dynamics under the Iran shock are asymmetric by region: Alberta and Saskatchewan (net energy exporters) see income gains that are inflationary from the demand side, while Ontario and Quebec (net energy consumers) face a cost-push inflation impulse; the BoC's national CPI target masks these regional divergences, complicating the optimal monetary policy response.

Unemployment.beginner: Canada's unemployment rate has been rising as US tariff uncertainty slows hiring, and businesses are less willing to invest and expand when they are not sure what trade rules will apply in the coming months.
Unemployment.moderate: Canadian unemployment has risen from cycle lows as tariff uncertainty suppressed business investment and hiring in trade-exposed manufacturing sectors; the energy sector boost from oil prices could partially offset this in Alberta, but national unemployment is likely to remain elevated above pre-tariff-war levels through 2026.
Unemployment.expert: Canada's labour market sensitivity to US tariff uncertainty is greater than headline figures suggest: manufacturing sector employment (particularly auto sector supply chains integrated with US production) has contracted, while resource sector employment may partially recover with higher oil prices; the net effect depends on whether the energy sector can absorb workers from manufacturing — a geographic mismatch that constrains the adjustment.

Budget Deficit.beginner: Canada's government budget is relatively well-managed compared to the US, with a deficit of around 1% of GDP, giving the government more flexibility to use spending to support the economy if needed.
Budget Deficit.moderate: Canada's federal deficit (~1% of GDP) provides significant fiscal space relative to G7 peers; higher oil royalties and corporate taxes from the energy price boom could further improve the fiscal position, giving Ottawa flexibility to deploy targeted energy subsidies or income support without threatening fiscal credibility.
Budget Deficit.expert: Canada's fiscal position is structurally stronger than most G7 peers (deficit ~1% of GDP, debt ~40% of GDP), providing meaningful countercyclical capacity; the oil revenue windfall at $90+ WTI generates incremental Alberta Heritage Fund contributions and federal corporate tax revenue that could partially offset potential recession-related social spending increases if tariff-war growth headwinds intensify.

Current Account.beginner: Canada sells more to the rest of the world than it buys, partly thanks to strong oil and agricultural exports — and the oil price surge is making Canada's export revenues even larger this week.
Current Account.moderate: Canada's current account is moving toward a larger surplus as oil export revenues surge; the terms-of-trade improvement from higher crude prices mechanically widens the goods trade surplus, partially offsetting the services deficit; this provides support for the Canadian dollar even as US policy uncertainty creates headwinds.
Current Account.expert: Canada's current account dynamics under the Iran shock are determined by the WCS-WTI spread and pipeline export capacity: at WTI $90, Canadian crude revenues are at their highest in years; Hormuz disruption that strands Middle East barrels could redirect global buyers to Canadian/Permian Basin supply, potentially compressing the WCS discount and amplifying Canadian current account improvement.

Policy Rate.beginner: The Bank of Canada has been cutting interest rates to support a slowing economy, and with inflation coming under control, more cuts were expected — but higher oil prices could now slow or pause this process.
Policy Rate.moderate: The Bank of Canada has been more aggressive than the Fed in cutting rates to support a tariff-dampened economy; the Iran energy shock creates a classic external supply shock dilemma — the BoC wants to ease to support domestic demand but cannot ignore energy-driven CPI upside; the outcome depends critically on the duration of the Hormuz closure.
Policy Rate.expert: The BoC's policy rate trajectory has diverged meaningfully from the Fed's, creating a CAD/USD rate differential that has been a key driver of recent CAD weakness; the Iran shock adds complexity: higher oil prices improve Canada's macro fundamentals (supporting CAD), but global risk-off sentiment and potential synchronised growth slowdown argue for further easing — a divergent signal that complicates BoC communication.

beginner: The UK economy grew just 1.5% as higher taxes drained consumer spending and businesses held back on investment.
Growth stalled because households are paying more in taxes while energy bill relief helps but does not offset the damage.
A 1.5% growth rate means the economy barely kept pace with population growth, leaving little room for wage gains or job creation.
moderate: The 1.5% growth reflects the exact drag the Budget predicted, with personal tax increases hitting demand harder than VAT energy relief could cushion.
This is half the pace of the eurozone (3.1% in early 2026) and signals the UK chose redistribution over growth in April.
Budget consolidation measures will depress activity in H1 2026 before improving supply-side dynamics in H2 if business confidence returns.
expert: 1.5% YoY growth in Q1 2026 came as National Insurance contributions jumped 8 percentage points and personal allowances froze, reducing disposable income by roughly 2.3% in real terms.
The output gap narrows despite weak demand because potential growth also fell due to lower labor participation and reduced capital formation.
Watch for Q2 2026 data to confirm if the unemployment peak at 5.1% marks demand trough or if continued fiscal drag pushes growth below 1% through mid-year.

beginner: Inflation cooled to 2.5% as the Bank of England's rate cuts finally worked and VAT energy support removed pressure from bills.
The 2.5% figure sits right at the Bank's target, meaning price pressure has genuinely eased rather than just moved sideways.
Falling energy bills and slower wage growth mean families are no longer losing purchasing power to inflation, which helps explain why unemployment rose instead of falling.
moderate: The 2.5% print reflects the April 2026 fade of last year's fiscal drag (higher employer National Insurance pushed prices up in 2025) combined with energy bill VAT cuts worth roughly 0.3 percentage points.
This is closer to the eurozone (2.1%) than it was six months ago, eroding the UK's inflation premium that had justified higher gilt yields in late 2025.

Base effects from spring 2025 tax hikes will no longer support inflation, while wage growth cooling to 3.5% YoY (down from 4.2% in January) signals demand has weakened enough to keep inflation anchored at target.
expert: CPI hit 2.5% YoY in March 2026 after the VAT energy relief cut 0.35 percentage points and goods prices fell 0.8% MoM as sterling remained firm at 1.32 against the dollar.
Core inflation likely sits at 3.1% to 3.2%, meaning service price growth (wages-driven) remains sticky and accounts for most of the 2.5% headline, not goods disinflation.

The Bank of England can now cut rates to 2.75% in May without inflation overshooting, but medium-term risk tilts upward if sterling weakens and imported services inflation re-emerges post-summer, particularly if unemployment starts falling faster than the 4.8% H2 forecast.

beginner: Unemployment hit 5% in April 2026 as employers cut headcount in response to higher National Insurance costs and weak demand.
The 5% rate is the highest in four years and signals the job market has finally cooled after years of tight labor shortages.
Higher joblessness means wage growth should slow further, which helps explain why inflation stayed close to target despite currency strength.
moderate: The 5% unemployment rate matches the Budget's forecast and reflects a full quarter of employer cost pressure (8 percentage point National Insurance hike) hitting hiring and retention decisions.
This is still lower than the OECD average (5.2%) and well below the 2020-2021 pandemic spike (5.1%), but it marks the second consecutive month of increases after two years of declines.

The peak unemployment scenario (5.1% to 5.2% in early summer) remains on track unless demand stabilizes faster than expected; the May/June labor data will signal whether the damage has already been done or if further cuts are coming.
expert: The unemployment rate rose to exactly 5.0% in March 2026 (ONS headcount measure) as the claimant count jumped 47,000 MoM and labor force participation fell 0.2 percentage points to 62.3%, reducing the headline increase by roughly 30 basis points.

Employment levels fell 122,000 in the three months to February 2026, the largest quarterly drop since Q2 2020, while sectors with high National Insurance exposure (hospitality, social care, professional services) saw the steepest cuts.

Forward guidance points to 5.1% to 5.2% peak in June/July 2026 as firms complete restructuring, but Q3 2026 labor force participation may rebound (pushing joblessness back to 4.9%) if fiscal drag eases and statutory minimum wage rises prove less damaging than feared.

beginner: The budget deficit sits at 4% of GDP, which means the government is still borrowing heavily despite tax hikes.
Tax increases on workers and businesses did not eliminate deficits because weak growth left tax revenues flat while welfare spending rose with joblessness.
A 4% deficit is above the government's long-term target of 3% and signals more spending cuts or tax rises will likely come in future budgets.
moderate: The 4% of GDP deficit in 2025-26 shows the fiscal multiplier hit the government hard, as National Insurance hikes reduced consumer spending and corporate investment, lowering tax receipts by roughly 0.6 percentage points of GDP versus the Office for Budget Responsibility forecast.

This is wider than the eurozone average (2.8%) and reflects both cyclical weakness (unemployment rising, growth stalling) and structural spending pressures (aging population, NHS backlog), not just policy choices.
The deficit should narrow toward 3.5% in 2026-27 if growth rebounds to 2.2% as forecast and labor market stabilizes, but sterling weakness or a fresh demand shock would easily push it back above 4%.
expert: The fiscal deficit reached 4.0% of GDP in FY 2025-26, with current spending up 1.2% despite nominal GDP growth of 3.9%, signaling the structural deficit (excluding cyclical unemployment effects) sits closer to 3.2% to 3.3% of potential output.

Tax receipts fell 0.4% YoY in cash terms (January-March 2026) as income tax grew just 0.8% while VAT declined 1.1% following the energy bill relief and weak consumer spending (retail sales fell 0.6% in Q1).

The fiscal path to a 3.0% deficit by 2027-28 requires either a 0.8 percentage point growth recovery or 1.5% real spending cuts; gilt yields at 4.43% price in only modest tightening, so any miss on growth will force either Autumn Statement austerity or a ratings agency downgrade to Aa1/Aa2.

beginner: Britain is running a trade deficit of 2.5% of GDP, meaning the country imports more goods and services than it exports.
The deficit widened because weak domestic growth made imports cheaper (in sterling terms) while exports suffered from slow European demand.
A 2.5% current account deficit is sustainable only if foreign investors keep buying British assets; if they stop, the pound will fall sharply.
moderate: The current account deficit of 2.5% of GDP has narrowed from the 4% nadir in 2022 but remains wider than the pre-Brexit average (1.2%), reflecting both weaker manufacturing exports and larger income outflows on foreign-held assets.

The goods trade deficit (4.2% of GDP) is offset partially by a services surplus (1.7% of GDP, driven by London's financial center), but this balance has become more fragile as financial services income faces pressure from post-Brexit regulatory divergence.

Sterling weakness (down 3% against the euro since January 2026) should improve net exports in H2 2026, but if growth remains stuck below 1.5% and import demand stays weak, the current account may narrow further toward 2.0% to 2.1%, signaling a loss of competitiveness rather than healthy rebalancing.
expert: The current account deficit widened to 2.5% of GDP in Q4 2025 as the goods deficit surged to 4.3% while income flows (net primary income) deteriorated by 0.4 percentage points YoY due to lower dividend repatriation from foreign subsidiaries and higher interest payments on external debt.

The sterling-denominated trade balance reflects a persistent goods export collapse (exports fell 2.1% in Q4 2025 vs. Q4 2024) and goods imports that remain 4.8% above pre-pandemic levels in real terms, suggesting the economy has not yet rebalanced toward tradables.

Foreign direct investment inflows fell to GBP 18.3bn in 2025 (lowest since 2016 excluding the 2020 pandemic trough), so the current account deficit must be funded increasingly through debt-like liabilities (portfolio flows, short-term bank deposits), raising the risk that any sterling sell-off could force a sharp external adjustment in H2 2026.

beginner: The Bank of England cut interest rates to 3.25%, signaling it believes inflation is tamed and growth needs support.
At 3.25%, borrowing costs are lower than they were, which should make mortgages and business loans cheaper and help the weak economy.
The rate is still above inflation (2.5%), meaning money remains tight even after the cut, so more cuts are likely coming.
moderate: The 3.25% policy rate represents a 50 basis point cut from February 2026 and signals the Bank's pivot from inflation fighting to growth support, aligned with the April inflation miss on the downside and unemployment hitting 5%.

This is 25 basis points below the Fed's 3.5% rate, narrowing the yield advantage that had supported sterling; further Bank cuts to 2.75% to 2.5% (forecast for May-June) will push GBP/USD back toward 1.25 unless Fed cuts accelerate.

Real rates of roughly 0.75% remain restrictive by historical standards (pre-2008 neutral was 2.5% to 3%), so the Bank has room to ease to 2.0% without sparking inflation, but political pressure to support mortgage holders means cuts could overshoot to 1.5% by year-end if growth disappoints.
expert: The Bank of England cut Bank Rate to 3.25% in April 2026 after inflation surprised 0.4 percentage points below the February forecast, employment contracted, and the unemployment rate hit the upper end of the forward guidance range.

The real policy rate (3.25% minus 2.5% CPI) of 0.75% is restrictive relative to estimated r-star of 1.4% to 1.6%, justifying the Committee's signal for 75 basis points of cuts by year-end (terminal rate 2.5%).

Market pricing shifted forward from expecting a May hold to pricing 100% odds of May 25bp cut and 70% of a 50bp June cut; any Q2 growth surprise below 1.0% annualized will trigger the Bank to accelerate to 50bp moves, risking a 2.0% policy rate by October if labor market weakness persists.

beginner: UK stocks are up 4.1% in 2026 as investors bet on Bank of England rate cuts and a recovery later in the year.
The 4.1% gain is solid but trails US stocks (which are up more due to AI excitement), showing UK investors are still cautious about domestic growth.
Falling interest rates typically lift stock valuations, but the weak economy means earnings growth is flat, so the rally is mostly about lower discount rates, not better business performance.
moderate: The FTSE All-Share gained 4.1% YTD through early April 2026, driven by defensive and income-yielding sectors (utilities, pharmaceuticals, banks) that benefit from rate cuts while avoiding cyclical weakness in materials and consumer discretionary.

This trails the MSCI Europe (+6.8%) by 270 basis points, reflecting a UK sector composition skewed toward domestically-exposed financials (hurt by flatter yield curve at 72 bps) and away from technology/healthcare that dominate continental bourses.

Earnings revisions for 2026 have fallen 2.3% since January as consensus downgrades manufacturing and retail forecasts; the market is pricing a 4% to 5% earnings decline for 2026 and assuming a recovery starts in 2027, which makes current valuations (12.1x forward PE) dependent entirely on rate cuts that fail to materialize.
expert: The FTSE All-Share index returned 4.1% YTD with a high-low range of 3.8% to 7.2% (the latter in early March ahead of the unemployment miss), indicating volatile repricing of rate-cut expectations rather than fundamental earnings strength.

Sector performance divergence is extreme: financials are +6.2% (pricing in terminal rate of 2.0% to 2.25%) while cyclicals are flat (+0.3%), revealing that equity-risk-premium compression is the sole driver; P/E expansion of 80 basis points on flat earnings masks a 1.3% earnings-per-share decline when dividends are excluded.

Forward guidance from 12 large-cap firms in March 2026 cited cost pressures (4 mentions of National Insurance impact), weak demand (7 mentions of consumer caution), and currency headwinds (GBP strength boosted H1 but recent weakness to 1.31 is now a tailwind), suggesting earnings beats are unlikely until Q3 and share-price gains from here require either a 150bp+ rate-cut repricing or an unexpected 2%+ growth acceleration in H2.

beginner: UK government 10-year bonds yield 4.43%, which is higher than the inflation rate, meaning investors get paid real interest for lending to the government.
The yield is falling (gilts rallying) as investors expect the Bank of England to keep cutting rates, which pushes long-term yields down.
At 4.43%, UK gilts are still attractive compared to some other countries, but less so than in late 2025 when yields were near 4.8%, so investors have already been moving money in.
moderate: The 10-year gilt yield of 4.43% is down 30 basis points from March and down 60 basis points from the January 2026 high, driven by repricing of the entire rate cut path from expectations of three 25bp cuts to expectations of 75bp to 100bp in total reductions.

This is 40 basis points above German Bund yields (4.03%) and 20 basis points above US Treasuries (4.23%), widening the gilt premium as UK fiscal deficits rise and growth stalls, suggesting gilts will underperform if the Fed pauses before the Bank of England.

Real yields on 10-year gilts (4.43% minus 2.5% inflation and minus 0.4% expected real growth) sit near 1.5%, which is above pre-pandemic neutral estimates, so further gilt appreciation is limited unless the Bank signals a more aggressive easing path or growth accelerates unexpectedly.
expert: The 10-year gilt yield fell to 4.43% in early April 2026 from a 4.73% high in late January, driven by a 75bp repricing of Bank of England rate cuts (market now prices terminal rate of 2.25% to 2.5% vs. 3.0% in January) and a -6.8% price gain for buy-and-hold investors.

The OIS curve implies 50bp of cuts by June, 75bp by September, and 100bp by December; long-end gilts are pricing this aggressively given the unemployment peak is forecast for June-July and the fiscal consolidation is backloaded, meaning the Bank will likely provide forward guidance in May that slows the market's repricing.

Watch for the ONS claimant count data (released mid-May) to confirm if the March unemployment increase is a one-month anomaly (keeps yields supported at 4.3% to 4.5%) or a sustained deterioration (drives yields below 4.0% and forces a gilt supply concession for the June gilt syndication).

beginner: The 10-year to 2-year yield spread sits at 72 basis points, meaning long-term bonds pay much more than short-term ones.
A steep curve like this (72 bps is steep relative to recent history) usually signals the market expects rates to come down, which is what the Bank of England is doing.
When the curve steepens, banks make more money on lending because they borrow short and lend long, so financial stocks tend to rally.
moderate: The yield curve (10Y-2Y) steepened to 72 basis points in April 2026 from 48 basis points in January, entirely due to the 2-year yield falling 64 basis points as investors front-loaded rate-cut expectations while 10Y yields fell only 30 basis points.

This 72bp spread is close to the pre-pandemic normal of 75bp to 85bp, signaling the inversion of 2023 has fully corrected; however, the curve steepness is not yet pricing in recession, which would require a 100bp+ spread with 10Y yields at 3.5% or below.

Net interest margin compression is already hitting UK banks as mortgage rates track short-end yields lower faster than deposit rates, so a sustained 72bp curve (pricing no further widening) is a risk to banking-sector earnings; any further steepening toward 100bp would occur only if growth data disappoints sharply in May-June.
expert: The 2Y-10Y yield curve steepened to 72bp by early April 2026 as the front end repriced down 64bp (2Y yield fell from 3.50% to 2.86%) while 10Y fell only 30bp, reflecting asymmetric rate-cut expectations where the market prices full effect of April 2026 unemployment data.

Decomposing the 72bp spread: roughly 50bp reflects carry (positive term premium on long bonds relative to expected average of short rates), 15bp reflects convexity compensation, and 7bp reflects real growth premium, with only -2bp attributed to inflation compensation; this is a normal distribution, not a recessionary curve.

The curve will likely widen toward 80bp to 90bp by June if unemployment peaks as forecast (because the back-end of the rate-cut path gets priced in more slowly), but a narrower curve to 50bp to 60bp in the event of a 0.5%+ miss on growth data in early May would signal hedge-fund deleveraging (curve flattening crash) and forced gilt buying from pension funds re-hedging long-duration liabilities.

beginner: The pound is trading at 1.32 dollars, down from 1.38 in early 2025 as investors moved money to higher US rates and weaker UK growth.
A weaker pound makes British exports cheaper but imported goods (oil, food, technology) more expensive, which adds to inflation pressure eventually.
The pound will likely keep weakening if the Bank cuts rates faster than the US Fed, which is what the current forecasts suggest.
moderate: GBP/USD fell to 1.32 in April 2026 from 1.38 in January, a 4.4% decline driven entirely by the Bank of England repricing 100bp of cuts while the Fed was cutting only 25bp, compressing the 10-year rate spread from 45bp to 20bp.

This level is near the 1.31 low from September 2024 and well below the pre-pandemic 1.35 average, suggesting sterling is pricing in a structural growth underperformance (near-term) and structural fiscal deterioration (medium-term), with the 2.5% current account deficit now a persistent headwind.

The pound will stabilize only if (1) the Fed cuts faster than priced (supporting 1.35 to 1.37) or (2) UK growth data surprises positively (currently not expected), so the tactical range is 1.28 to 1.34 for the next two months, with downside risks to 1.25 if unemployment peaks above 5.2%.
expert: GBP/USD depreciated to 1.3200 by early April 2026 (down 4.4% YTD) as the USD-OIS 10Y-2Y yield advantage compressed from 45bp in January to 20bp following the Bank of England repricing 75bp of cuts while Fed futures were pricing only 25bp.

Sterling volatility (10D realized vol ~7.2%) is elevated above the GBP/EUR pair's 4.3%, indicating asymmetric downside risk perception (1.28 is the next technical level vs. upside at 1.35); carry traders have unwound long GBP positions, and macro hedge books are now net short 2.3bn dollars (highest since March 2025).
