At 6.7% of GDP, the total deficit is 150bps wider than the central bank's growth-adjusted neutral rate, meaning fiscal policy is additive despite 12% policy rates, a contradiction that forces the bank to remain hawkish to prevent currency decompression.

The fiscal math is brutal: to stabilize debt at 85% of GDP (the implied ceiling), Brazil needs to swing the primary balance to surplus by 2.5-3% of GDP within 18 months; if that fails and growth stays at 1.7%, expect debt to breach 82% by 2027 and trigger a sovereign downgrade.

beginner: Brazil's current account deficit sits at 2.6% of GDP, which means the country is borrowing more from abroad than it earns through trade and services, a structural vulnerability.

With the fiscal crisis at home and a 12% policy rate still not attractive enough to offset the deficit, Brazil needs foreign investment to keep the lights on, but investors are getting nervous about the budget spiral.
A 2.6% current account deficit is manageable if growth accelerates, but at 1.7% growth with a worsening fiscal picture, that deficit could widen as capital inflows slow.
moderate: Brazil's 2.6% current account deficit reflects weak goods exports (commodity prices down 8% YTD) offset partially by services and remittances, but the deficit is now structural rather than cyclical because commodity terms-of-trade have reset lower.

The current account gap (2.6% of GDP) is sustainable only if the central bank can attract dollar inflows through higher rates (12% policy rate paid), but with growth at 1.7% and fiscal deficits blowing out, the risk premium is rising.

Historically, Brazil runs a surplus or near-balance; a 2.6% deficit at peak policy rates signals commodity exports have lost competitiveness (real effective exchange rate near five-year highs) and capital goods imports are eating the surplus.
expert: The 2.6% current account deficit financed by FDI and portfolio flows now depends entirely on the 12% policy rate spread versus global rates (US 10Y at 4.2%); if Brazil cuts to 10.5% before fiscal reforms appear credible, the deficit widens to 3.2-3.5% as rate differentials collapse.

Commodity exports remain under pressure (iron ore down 6%, agricultural prices down 3% YTD), while the real effective exchange rate (near 105, five-year high) is eroding export competitiveness faster than the current account deterioration reflects, suggesting a lag-weighted decline ahead.

Monitor dollar inflow trends in May-June BACEN data; if portfolio flows fall below $500 million per month while FDI remains flat, Brazil will need to defend the current account through either rate hikes or capital controls, both of which break the growth outlook.

beginner: The central bank holds rates at 12%, the highest in the developing world right now, because it's terrified that cutting rates could spark inflation or cause the currency to collapse.
At 12%, borrowing costs are so high that Brazilian companies and families can barely afford to invest or buy homes, which is why growth is stuck at 1.7% even though inflation (4.2%) is under control.
The bank is trapped: it can't cut rates without risking a currency crisis, but keeping rates at 12% will eventually trigger a recession and push unemployment above 7%.
moderate: The 12% policy rate reflects a 780bps premium over the US 10Y (4.2%), a gap that historically signaled currency devaluation risk or political instability; here it's fiscal fear, as investors demand compensation for potential sovereign rating downgrades.

The real policy rate (12% minus 4.2% CPI) of 7.8% is the highest in emerging markets and well above the long-run neutral rate (3.5-4%), confirming the central bank is using rates as a fiscal stabilizer because the government won't cut spending.

The negative yield curve (10Y at 13.8% versus 12% policy rate) signals growth recession fears and is a historically reliable recession signal; the central bank faces a choice between easing into recession or tightening further to defend the currency.
expert: At 12%, the policy rate is 780bps over the US 10Y and 570bps over Brazil's own 10Y real rate (13.8% nominal minus 4.2% CPI equals 9.6% real), the second-widest real policy rate gap globally and unsustainable beyond Q3 given 1.7% growth.

The inverted yield curve (negative 140bps) reflects expectations of a 200-250bps rate cut cycle starting in June if fiscal news stabilizes; the central bank's guidance points to 11% by August, but that cut cycle depends entirely on Congress passing a fiscal framework by end-April.

If fiscal reforms stall and Congress misses the April deadline, expect the central bank to hold at 12% through Q3, pushing the real policy rate to 8.2% in real terms and triggering a 150-200bps widening of the output gap; watch May FOCAM guidance for the pivot signal.

beginner: Brazilian stocks are up 17.1% so far this year in local currency, a sharp rally, but most of that gain came in January when hope for rate cuts and fiscal reforms ran high.

The rally masks a divergence: large-cap, dollar-earning stocks (like oil companies) are up 19%, while domestic-focused, rate-sensitive stocks (like banks and retailers) are flat or down, showing investors don't trust the growth story.
Watch out: if the central bank signals it won't cut rates soon, or if fiscal reforms look unlikely, this rally will reverse fast, and stocks could fall 15-20% by year-end.
moderate: The 17.1% YTD gain in local currency masks a 13.88% gain in USD terms, showing the real appreciated 3% versus the dollar in Q1, a move that typically fades as fiscal concerns resurface and capital flows reverse.

Bank stocks (20% of the Bovespa index) are up only 8% YTD despite the broad rally, a tell-tale sign of recession fears and margin compression from the 12% policy rate; energy and materials stocks (30% of index) carry the rally on commodity and export hopes.

The rally peaked in mid-February at 18.5% gains; the March pullback and flat April performance reflect a loss of confidence in the fiscal reform timeline and growing doubts about the central bank's ability to cut rates without triggering a currency crisis.
expert: The 17.1% YTD gain masks a 410bps divergence between large-cap (up 19%, USD hedged) and small-cap (up 11%), with banks flatline at 8% despite lower unemployment and stable credit growth, signaling a sharp reassessment of earnings durability under continued 12% rates.

Valuation expansion (P/E multiple up 8% YTD) accounts for 9 of the 17.1% gains while earnings growth is near zero; if fiscal reforms fail and the central bank holds rates, the multiple compression will offset the currency benefit, sending the index to 110,000 (minus 18% from current 134,500).

Monitor April earnings guidance from Itau, Bradesco, and Vale for signals on cost inflation (12% funding rates) and capex cuts; if three or more megacaps cut 2026 earnings guidance by 5%+, expect a retest of the 120,000 level (minus 11%) and a rotation toward dollar-hedged plays.

beginner: Brazil's 10-year government bond yields 13.8%, an extremely high rate that reflects investor fear about the fiscal crisis and debt spiral.

That 13.8% yield is the price of Brazil's dysfunction: the government can't borrow cheaply because nobody trusts that the budget deficit will shrink, so every new bond issuance costs more than the last.
If yields climb to 14.5%, the debt service bill explodes and forces even deeper spending cuts, which would push growth even lower and make unemployment worse.
moderate: At 13.8%, Brazil's 10Y yield is 960bps above the US 10Y (4.2%), the widest spread versus the US since 2020, and signals that credit markets have priced in a 60% probability of a downgrade to below-investment-grade within 24 months.

The yield has climbed 80bps in the past three months as fiscal data deteriorated (primary deficit jump), while the real depreciated 3% versus the dollar, creating a vicious cycle of higher borrowing costs and currency losses on external debt.

The curve inversion (10Y at 13.8% versus 12% policy rate) is extreme and historically signals either a recession (growth compresses to 0-1%) or a policy reversal (rate cuts to 10%+); the central bank can't sustain this contradiction beyond June without a fiscal reform credible signal.
expert: The 13.8% 10Y yield is 960bps above the US 10Y and reflects a compound effect: 200bps for fiscal deterioration (primary deficit from surplus to R$100.6 billion deficit), 150bps for currency devaluation risk (USD/BRL touching 5.30 lows), and 610bps for the structural 12% policy rate premium needed to defend the real.

Duration risk is acute: if the central bank cuts to 10% (down 200bps from current 12%) while yields stay flat, the bond market loses 2% of capital immediately; the 10-2 curve inversion of minus 140bps is a recession symptom that precedes a 300-400bps duration rally.

The break-even point: if fiscal reforms (Congress vote) materialize by late-April and the primary deficit outlook improves to minus 4% of GDP by end-2026, 10Y yields compress to 12.5% and fuel a 4-5% rally in bond prices; failure means yields spike to 14.5% and trigger forced selling by local funds.

beginner: Brazil's yield curve is inverted by 140 basis points, meaning short-term borrowing costs (12%) are higher than long-term costs (13.8%), which is completely backwards and signals a recession is coming.
When the yield curve inverts, companies stop investing because they can't borrow cheaply long-term, and people stop buying homes because mortgages are expensive; that's why growth is stuck at 1.7%.

A normal yield curve would have long-term rates higher than short-term rates to reward investors for locking money away; Brazil's inversion means investors expect the central bank to cut rates dramatically, which only happens if a recession forces it.
moderate: The minus 140bps inversion (10Y at 13.8% versus 12% policy rate) is Brazil's most extreme since 2018 and signals that bond markets expect the central bank to cut rates by 200+ basis points within 12 months, implying a recession.

Historically, Brazil's yield curve inverts 3-4 quarters before GDP growth turns negative; the last inversion (2017-2018) preceded a 50bps recession bounce, but current fiscal deficits are much larger, so the next downturn could be sharper.

The inversion persists because the central bank can't cut rates (fiscal crisis) and can't keep them high indefinitely (growth collapse); this trap usually resolves through either a currency devaluation (forcing higher rates) or a fiscal shock (forcing rate cuts despite inflation risk).
expert: At minus 140bps, the 2-10 curve inversion is the most inverted since 2018 (minus 150bps pre-recession) and reflects the market pricing a 200-250bps rate cut cycle by end-2026; this scenario requires the primary deficit to stabilize below minus 3% of GDP by Q3, a bar the government has not yet cleared.

The inversion mechanics: the central bank holds 12% (despite 1.7% growth and 4.2% CPI) to anchor the real against currency devaluation (USD/BRL at 5.17), while the 10Y is pricing a 10% equilibrium rate six quarters out, implying a 15% cumulative shock either to growth or fiscal credibility.

Curve normalization signals: watch for a 2-10 curve steepening back to plus 50bps by July; that move requires either a central bank rate cut to 11.5% (paired with fiscal reform credibility) or a 10Y yield drop to 12.8% (paired with currency stabilization). If neither occurs by August, expect a retest of the minus 180bps inversion lows and a recession consensus.

beginner: The US dollar buys 5.17 Brazilian reals right now, near the highest level in five years, which means the real is weak and getting weaker as investors lose confidence in Brazil's fiscal situation.
A weak real makes imports expensive (cars, gasoline, phones all cost more), pushes inflation up, and forces the central bank to keep rates at 12% even though that kills economic growth.
If the dollar pushes above 5.30, foreign investors will demand even higher Brazilian bond yields, creating a vicious cycle of currency weakness, higher rates, and slower growth.
moderate: USD/BRL at 5.17 is near the five-year high (5.31 in 2020) and reflects the 780bps interest rate differential (12% policy rate versus 4.2% US 10Y) being overwhelmed by fiscal crisis concerns; the real has lost 7% of value since end-2024.

The currency weakness is structural: the current account deficit (2.6% of GDP) and capital outflows from rising sovereign risk premium outpace the carry trade benefits of the 12% policy rate, a pattern that historically precedes deeper depreciation.

The real effective exchange rate (versus peers) is near five-year highs at 105, making Brazilian exports less competitive; a further 5% real depreciation (to 5.45 USD/BRL) would trigger imported inflation of 200bps and force the central bank to defend at 12.5% rates rather than cut.
expert: USD/BRL at 5.17 reflects a 780bps carry premium (12% policy rate minus 4.2% US 10Y) being arbitraged away by a fiscal risk premium of 350bps (implied by bond yields and CDS spreads); the real is weaker than fundamentals support because markets doubt the government's willingness to reform.

The depreciation trajectory (5.10 end-2024 to 5.17 now) is mild by emerging market crisis standards, but CDS on Brazil 5-year debt (240bps) signals another 8-12% depreciation move (to 5.45-5.55) is priced if fiscal reforms fail by May 2026, making USD/BRL a crowded short trade.

Monitor April-May capital flow data (BACEN IDP): if portfolio inflows fall below $300 million per month while the current account deficit widens to 2.9%, expect a test of 5.40 USD/BRL by June; if that breaks with the central bank holding at 12% rates, a cascade to 5.60+ becomes likely and forces emergency fiscal measures.

beginner: Brazilian stocks are up 13.88% in US dollar terms this year, which is weaker than the 17.1% local currency gain because the real weakened 3% against the dollar.
For a US investor, the rally is real but smaller: they got 13.88% stock gains but gave back 3% to currency depreciation, netting only 13.88% of the move instead of the full 17.1%.

If the real keeps weakening (toward 5.40-5.50), US investors will keep losing currency value even if the Brazilian stock index climbs further, which is why smart international investors are hedging the real.
moderate: The 13.88% USD return trails the 17.1% local return by 310bps due to 3% real depreciation (USD/BRL 5.00 to 5.17), a drag that reflects structural capital outflows and fiscal risk premium as foreign investors reduce Brazil exposure.

In USD terms, the rally is driven entirely by large-cap energy and materials stocks that earn dollars (Vale, Petrobras up 19-22%), while domestic financials and consumer stocks are flat to negative for US-based investors due to both weak local earnings and currency headwinds.

The divergence signals hedging is expensive and rarely worth it: the 3% currency loss was smaller than historical precedent (2020-2021 average depreciation was 8% during fiscal crises), suggesting capital outflows may be slowing despite rising sovereign risk.
expert: The 310bps gap between 17.1% local and 13.88% USD returns reflects 3% real depreciation and 20bps in carry cost from USD funding, decomposing as follows: 80% of the return came from multiple expansion (lower discount rates from rate-cut expectations), 20% from earnings growth (near zero for domestic names), and the currency drag offset 3% of total gains.

The Bovespa (BRL) is up 17.1% with a 500bps P/E multiple expansion (12.5x forward to 13.0x), while the Bovespa in USD terms (13.88% gain) reflects a 200bps multiple contraction when restated in dollars due to the currency weakness, a sign that US investors are rotating out of duration plays.

If real depreciation accelerates to 5.5 (plus 6% move from current 5.17), the USD return compresses to 10.5% despite the local 17% rally; this happens if capital outflows spike in May following fiscal reform delays, creating a window to rotate into dollar-hedged large-caps (Vale, Petrobras) before the currency inflection.

beginner: Brazil's government debt just jumped to 79.2% of GDP, and the budget swung from a surplus into a massive deficit. This means Brazil is spending way more than it takes in, and creditors are starting to worry.
Brazil added only 255,320 formal jobs last month, falling short of expectations and suggesting the job market is cooling down. Fewer jobs mean less consumer spending and slower growth ahead.
Wholesale prices actually fell 0.25% month-on-month, which sounds good but signals weak demand across the economy. When businesses cannot raise prices, it means they are struggling to sell.
moderate: Brazil's gross debt surged to 79.2% of GDP while the primary budget swung from a R$40 billion surplus to a R$100.6 billion deficit, a shocking deterioration that signals fiscal discipline has broken. The shift reflects both revenue shortfalls and expenditure pressures that the government cannot control.

Job creation collapsed to 255,320 (below the 270,000 consensus), suggesting the labor market is tightening at precisely the moment when the central bank is holding rates at 15.0%. The weakness hints that the economy is already slowing faster than the 1.7% full-year forecast implies.

PPI deflation of 0.25% month-on-month indicates wholesale price pressure is easing, but the inflation rate at 3.81% remains slightly below the 4.2% forecast. The central bank faces a credibility crisis as fiscal deterioration forces it to keep rates high despite slowing growth.
expert: Gross debt jumped 50 basis points to 79.2% of GDP while net debt hit 65.5%, accompanied by a primary deficit swing of R$140.6 billion quarter-over-quarter. The fiscal deterioration is structural, not cyclical, and signals the government's inability to manage mandatory spending without revenue hikes or growth.

CAGED job creation missed consensus by 14,680 positions, falling to 255,320, while PPI deflated 0.25% month-on-month. These signals suggest the economy is decelerating faster than the 1.7% full-year forecast, tightening the real growth-inflation corridor available to the SELIC at 15.0%.

The real policy rate (15.0% minus 3.81% inflation) sits at 11.19%, among the highest globally, yet the primary deficit and debt trajectory continue to worsen. This points to a medium-term fiscal dominance problem where the central bank's credibility depends on eventual fiscal consolidation, not just rate hikes.

fxRegime.label: Managed Float
fxRegime.beginner: Brazil’s real floats freely on currency markets, but the central bank (BCB) steps in when moves become extreme. USD/BRL shows how many reais you need to buy one US dollar. At 5.22, one dollar costs about 5.2 reais. Brazil’s very high interest rates attract foreign investors seeking better returns — this is called a ‘carry trade’ — which can support the real, but political or fiscal worries can cause sharp sell-offs.
fxRegime.moderate: Managed float with active BCB intervention via FX swaps (NDF-settled) and spot auctions. The real is one of the most traded EM currencies, driven by: the Selic-Fed funds differential (~11pp, supporting carry), commodity exposure (soybeans, iron ore, oil), and fiscal/political risk sentiment. BRL vol (~16-17% annualized) reflects the tension between attractive carry and periodic fiscal/political risk-off episodes.
fxRegime.expert: Managed float with intervention primarily via USD-settled FX swap programme (notional ~$100bn outstanding) rather than spot reserves. BCB uses swaps to manage forward curve steepness and hedge corporate external debt rollover risk. Reserve position ~$350bn provides ample cover (~14 months imports) and exceeds Guidotti-Greenspan threshold. Key BRL dynamics: (1) carry attractiveness — Selic-SOFR spread ~11pp supports positioning but creates convex downside risk on unwind; (2) terms of trade — BRL correlated with commodity index (~0.5) given export mix (soybeans, iron ore, oil, protein); (3) fiscal risk premium — pre-election spending risk and debt trajectory keep the BRL risk premium elevated vs model-implied fair value.

GDP Growth.beginner: Brazil's economy is benefiting from the oil price surge, as Petrobras produces large amounts of oil and the higher prices mean more revenue for the company and the Brazilian government — but high interest rates at home are still a brake on overall economic growth.
GDP Growth.moderate: Brazil's GDP growth benefits from higher Petrobras revenues and agricultural export strength (soybeans, corn), but is constrained by the world's highest real interest rates (Selic above 13%), fiscal concerns under President Lula, and a BRL that has been weakening on risk-off sentiment despite improving terms of trade.
GDP Growth.expert: Brazil's growth is caught between two opposing forces: the commodity export windfall (oil, agriculture) improving the external accounts and Petrobras fiscal contributions, and the Lula government's fiscal expansion tendencies that have kept the Selic elevated as the BCB resists easing that could trigger FX depreciation and BRL-denominated inflation.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: Brazilian inflation has been stubbornly high, partly because of the weak currency and partly because of rising food prices, and higher oil prices from the Iran conflict could push fuel and goods prices higher, adding to cost-of-living pressure.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: Brazilian CPI has been running above the BCB's 3% target amid BRL weakness (FX passthrough) and food price pressures; the Iran oil shock creates upside CPI risk via domestic fuel prices (Petrobras pricing policy) and logistics costs — but Petrobras's pricing formula may absorb some of the shock if the government exercises its shareholder influence to delay passthrough.
Inflation (CPI).expert: Brazil's inflation dynamics are fundamentally linked to the BRL exchange rate via FX passthrough (estimated at 0.2-0.3pp of CPI per 10% BRL depreciation); the Iran risk-off environment that typically weakens BRL creates a secondary inflationary impulse on top of direct energy price increases; any signal of political interference in BCB independence would amplify both BRL weakness and inflationary expectations.

Unemployment.beginner: Brazil's unemployment rate has been falling to around 6.5-7%, relatively low by historical standards, helped by growth in agriculture, construction, and services — though quality jobs with social benefits remain scarce for many workers.
Unemployment.moderate: Brazil's unemployment at ~6.5% is at a cyclical low, supported by agricultural employment (record harvests) and government-linked construction projects; the oil price windfall could support Petrobras employment and supply-chain jobs in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo states, partially offsetting any weakening in manufacturing from BRL volatility.
Unemployment.expert: Brazil's labour market is structurally characterised by high informality (40%+ of the workforce), which creates a buffer against cyclical shocks (informal workers absorb adjustment without appearing in unemployment statistics) but limits productivity growth and wage-setting efficiency; the oil-related employment boost is concentrated in formal high-wage jobs (Petrobras, engineering services) with limited aggregate demand multiplier effects for the broader economy.

Budget Deficit.beginner: Brazil's government is spending more than it earns, with a persistent fiscal deficit, and investors worry that the Lula government may expand spending further — which could weaken the currency and push up inflation.
Budget Deficit.moderate: Brazil's fiscal deficit (primary + interest: near 7-8% of GDP on consolidated basis) reflects the fundamental tension between constitutional spending mandates, social program expansion, and debt dynamics; Petrobras dividends (boosted by high oil prices) provide incremental fiscal revenue, but the structural spending trajectory remains unsustainable without reform.
Budget Deficit.expert: Brazil's fiscal framework is constrained by constitutional spending rules and the BCB's inflation target mandate; the Petrobras dividend windfall at $90+ oil provides a one-time fiscal improvement estimated at R$30-50bn (additional 0.3-0.5% of GDP) that could temporarily reduce the primary deficit — but this does not alter the structural deficit dynamic that requires entitlement reform the Lula government has been reluctant to pursue before elections.

Current Account.beginner: Brazil is becoming a larger oil exporter, and the surge in oil prices means the country is earning significantly more from its energy exports — improving the trade balance and potentially supporting the Brazilian real.
Current Account.moderate: Brazil's current account is improving mechanically from higher Petrobras oil export revenues at $90+ WTI; the agricultural export surplus (soybeans, corn at elevated prices) provides additional support; but Brazil's structural current account deficit from services means the improvement may be smaller than commodity price movements suggest.
Current Account.expert: Brazil's oil export capacity is growing structurally as Santos Basin pre-salt developments ramp up; at $90+ WTI, Brazilian breakeven costs of $35-40/barrel generate extraordinary economic rent; the key risk is that Lula government shareholder pressure on Petrobras's fuel pricing policy (to limit domestic inflation) could reduce Petrobras's upstream profitability and dividend capacity, partially negating the fiscal windfall from higher global prices.

Policy Rate.beginner: Brazil has some of the world's highest interest rates, with the Selic rate above 13%, making borrowing extremely expensive — and the central bank has been cautious about cutting rates because of persistent inflation and currency weakness.
Policy Rate.moderate: Brazil's Selic rate above 13% reflects the BCB's response to persistent inflation and BRL weakness; the Iran shock creates conflicting signals for the BCB: higher oil-driven CPI argues for holding, but positive terms-of-trade improvement (oil revenues) argues for easing; the risk-off BRL depreciation typically tips the BCB toward holding to defend currency credibility.
Policy Rate.expert: Brazil's real interest rate (Selic minus CPI) is among the world's highest, creating a significant competitiveness cost for the domestic economy; the BCB's rate-setting is constrained by the constant threat of capital outflows if real rates fall too quickly toward EM peer levels; the Iran shock that strengthens the current account (higher oil exports) but weakens the capital account (risk-off outflows) creates net BOP uncertainty the BCB will resolve by keeping rates elevated — effectively exporting the real income cost of the oil shock to Brazilian households and businesses through tight monetary conditions.

beginner: Russia's economy grew just 1.2% last year, meaning sanctions and military spending are weighing heavily despite Moscow claiming strength.
Growth this weak suggests Russia is burning through reserves to fund the war rather than building sustainable economic momentum.
Watch whether growth turns negative in 2026, which would signal that isolation and capital flight are finally crushing the fundamentals.
moderate: Russia posted 1.2% growth while the global average sits around 2.5%, revealing how much sanctions have isolated it from world trade.
This tepid pace reflects massive military spending (estimated 5-6% of GDP) crowding out productive investment, compared to Russia's pre-2022 average of 1.8% growth.
The New START expiration in February 2026 removes a negotiating lever; if Russia's growth stays below 1.5% through mid-year, pressure for economic reforms could mount.
expert: Russia's 1.2% YoY growth masks a sharp deceleration from Q1 2024 momentum, signaling that monetary tightening at 12.5% and capital controls are finally binding.
Real GDP adjusted for inflation (1.2% nominal minus 4.7% CPI) implies contraction in real activity, suggesting hidden recessionary pressure beneath headline numbers.
Forward signal: if the Central Bank cuts rates to below 12% in response, expect a rebound attempt; if not, 0-0.5% growth in H2 2026 is the base case.

beginner: Inflation at 4.7% means prices are rising faster than Russia wants, forcing the central bank to keep interest rates painfully high at 12.5%.
This tells you Russia still has goods shortages and currency pressure despite two years of adaptation to sanctions.
If inflation stays above 4%, the central bank won't cut rates, which keeps mortgages and business loans expensive and slows growth further.
moderate: Russia's 4.7% inflation is elevated for a country with its own currency and capital controls; pre-2022 it averaged 2-3%, showing persistent pricing power struggles.
The gap between the 12.5% policy rate and 4.7% inflation creates a real rate of 7.8%, which is historically very restrictive and explains the 1.2% growth.
Watch for renewed ruble depreciation if inflation crosses 5.5%; the Central Bank has signaled it won't tolerate double-digit CPI again.
expert: CPI at 4.7% sits in the upper band of the Central Bank's 4-5% comfort zone, suggesting tightening has nearly achieved its goal despite the 12.5% nominal rate.
Core inflation (stripping food and energy) likely runs 4.2-4.4%, indicating that wage-driven demand remains the marginal driver, not supply shocks alone.
Next move: if monthly CPI prints accelerate above 0.4% (April-May), expect the Central Bank to signal a hold above 12.5%; if sub-0.3%, cuts could begin in Q3 2026.

beginner: At 2.5%, unemployment is almost artificially low because hundreds of thousands of working-age men are conscripted or have fled the country.
This number doesn't capture the real pain, which is severe labor shortages in key sectors and wage inflation pressuring employers.
If conscription slows or the war ends, unemployment could spike sharply as soldiers re-enter the labor market.
moderate: Russia's 2.5% unemployment is the tightest in European data, but reflects demography (war deaths, emigration of 500k+ since 2022) rather than economic health.
Pre-2022 Russian unemployment averaged 4.5-5.5%, so the current reading is a supply-side collapse, not demand strength.
Wage growth has accelerated to 7-8% annually to compensate for labor scarcity, which feeds back into inflation and explains why the central bank cannot ease.

Decomposing the curve: the 130bp gap between policy and 2Y rates signals the market expects cuts to begin by Q4 2026; the 200bp premium of 10Y over 2Y reflects tail-risk hedging (war escalation, default).

Signal: if the 2Y-10Y spread widens to +100bps or more, the market is pricing a durable rate-cut cycle; if it compresses below +50bps, it signals sustained high-for-long rates and recession risk above 50%.

fxRegime.label: Managed Float (Capital Controls)
fxRegime.beginner: Russia's ruble is officially a 'floating' currency, but in practice the government heavily controls it. After Western sanctions froze Russia's foreign reserves in 2022, Moscow imposed strict rules: exporters must convert most of their foreign earnings into rubles, and there are limits on how much money can leave the country. USD/RUB shows how many rubles one US dollar buys. At 81, one dollar costs 81 rubles — much stronger than the 110+ level seen in late 2024, but this strength is largely engineered by capital controls rather than genuine market confidence.
fxRegime.moderate: Managed float with extensive capital controls imposed post-2022 sanctions. The CBR intervenes indirectly via mandatory FX conversion requirements (80% of export proceeds) rather than direct market operations, since ~$300bn of reserves remain frozen in Western jurisdictions. The onshore USD/RUB rate (~81) diverges from offshore NDF pricing, reflecting convertibility risk and sanctions premium. Ruble volatility is artificially suppressed by capital controls but subject to periodic dislocations when enforcement changes or oil price shocks hit. The effective FX regime is closer to a managed peg maintained by administrative measures rather than reserve-based intervention.
fxRegime.expert: De facto dual exchange rate regime masked as a managed float. Onshore rate (~81/USD) is administratively managed via: (1) mandatory 80% FX conversion for exporters; (2) restrictions on cross-border capital transfers; (3) informal 'guidance' to state-owned banks on FX positioning. Offshore NDF market (thin liquidity, wide bid-ask) reflects true risk-adjusted convertibility value. The 45% appreciation in 2025 is a policy choice — it contains imported inflation and signals stability, but at the cost of fiscal revenue compression (each 1 RUB appreciation costs ~₽150bn in annual oil revenue) and export competitiveness erosion. The CBR's usable reserves (~$250bn after subtracting frozen assets and gold held domestically) provide limited ammunition for genuine intervention; the regime's stability depends entirely on capital control enforcement and commodity price levels.

GDP Growth.beginner: Russia's economy has been kept running largely by military spending and energy revenues, but with the shadow fleet of tankers under increasing pressure and the ongoing cost of the Ukraine war, Russia's longer-term economic sustainability remains questionable.
GDP Growth.moderate: Russia's GDP growth (officially positive, driven by defence spending and wartime production) benefits from higher oil revenues at $90+ Urals-equivalent, but the economy's structural distortions — inflation, labor shortages from mobilisation, sanctioned technology gaps — mean higher oil prices mask rather than resolve the underlying fragility.
GDP Growth.expert: Russia's fiscal breakeven at ~$70-80/barrel Urals means current prices are above breakeven, providing National Wealth Fund breathing room; but Russian economic data is severely impaired by wartime opacity, and independent estimates suggest significant misallocation: military production crowds out civilian investment, inflation is above the CBR's 4% target, and real wages in the civilian economy are being eroded by defence-sector demand for labour.

Inflation (CPI).beginner: Russia's inflation has been high, well above the central bank's 4% target, pushed up by government spending on the war, sanctions limiting imported goods, and a weakening ruble — and the Iran conflict adds further uncertainty.
Inflation (CPI).moderate: Russian CPI has been running materially above the CBR's 4% target (estimated 8-12% depending on methodology) due to wartime fiscal expansion, import substitution failures, and ruble depreciation; the Iran conflict creates contradictory forces — higher oil revenues are ruble-positive (reducing import inflation) but global risk-off could weaken the ruble via capital flight.
Inflation (CPI).expert: Russia's inflation measurement is methodologically compromised by wartime price controls, the disappearance of sanctioned product categories from the CPI basket, and the divergence between official and black-market exchange rates; the FRED series for Russian CPI (RUSCPIALLMINMEI) remains active and provides one of the few internationally benchmarked data points, but its reliability as a measure of ordinary Russians' cost-of-living experience is increasingly questioned by independent economists.

Unemployment.beginner: Russia's official unemployment is very low — near historic lows — but this is misleading; many workers have been drafted into the military, and severe labour shortages in civilian industries are pushing up wages in ways that fuel inflation.
Unemployment.moderate: Russia's reported unemployment near 2.5% reflects military mobilisation absorbing civilian workers, not genuine full employment; the labour shortage in civilian manufacturing, logistics, and agriculture is generating double-digit wage inflation in some sectors that is contributing to above-target CPI and complicating the CBR's inflation management.
Unemployment.expert: Russia's labour market is distorted by the largest military mobilisation since WWII: approximately 600,000-800,000 troops deployed creates a structural labour supply reduction in civilian industries; the resulting wage pressure in civilian sectors (construction, agriculture, logistics) represents a form of forced supply-side constraint that resembles an adverse labour supply shock — distinct from demand-side dynamics that conventional monetary policy can address.

Budget Deficit.beginner: Russia's government is spending heavily on its military operations, and while high oil prices help fund this, the costs of the Ukraine war are draining the country's savings and creating long-term fiscal pressures.
Budget Deficit.moderate: Russia's oil revenues at above-breakeven Urals prices reduce the pace of National Wealth Fund depletion; however, military spending (estimated at 6-7% of GDP officially, possibly higher including classified items) creates a structural deficit that is only sustainable if oil prices remain elevated and the NWF maintains sufficient liquidity.
Budget Deficit.expert: Russia's fiscal position is uniquely sensitive to the Urals-Brent discount: Western sanctions and shadow fleet logistics costs have historically maintained a $10-20 discount; if the Iran conflict increases global tanker demand and reduces shadow fleet operating freedom (US naval presence, increased insurance scrutiny), the effective discount could widen even as Brent rises, compressing Russia's net oil revenue despite headline oil price strength.

Current Account.beginner: Russia earns significant revenue from selling oil and gas to China, India, and other countries that have not joined Western sanctions, and higher oil prices mean more income coming into the country — though the shadow tanker fleet faces increasing scrutiny.
Current Account.moderate: Russia's current account has recovered from post-invasion lows as the shadow fleet enabled continued oil exports at discounted Urals prices; at current price levels, the current account surplus is meaningful, but the Iran conflict introduces uncertainty about the shadow fleet's operational freedom if the US military's Gulf presence intensifies enforcement of secondary sanctions.
Current Account.expert: Russia's oil export supply chain depends critically on the shadow tanker fleet (estimated 700+ vessels) enabling price-cap-circumventing sales to India and China; the Iran conflict creates several risk vectors: US secondary sanction enforcement may intensify as part of Middle East campaign strategic logic; insurers may become more restrictive about shadow fleet coverage; and Indian state refiners may be constrained in increasing Russian imports while managing their own energy supply emergency — all potentially compressing Russia's realised export volumes and prices.

Policy Rate.beginner: Russia's central bank has kept interest rates very high to try to control inflation caused by military spending and the economic distortions of sanctions, but high rates are also hurting Russian businesses that need to borrow to invest.
Policy Rate.moderate: The CBR's policy rate (likely 16-21% based on recent history; FRED data available) is set in a wartime context where conventional monetary transmission is impaired: high rates are intended to control inflation and defend the ruble, but the military spending impulse is itself inflationary and not rate-sensitive, making the CBR's task difficult in both theory and practice.
Policy Rate.expert: Russia's monetary policy operates in a command-economy hybrid: the CBR has maintained de jure independence but faces political pressure to balance war-financing needs (lower rates for state banks funding defence contracts) with inflation control (high rates) and ruble stability (high rates); the effective transmission of policy rate changes is severely impaired by the prevalence of subsidised state credit for defence-related production — creating a dual-rate economy where headline CBR rates reflect anti-inflation intent but actual financing conditions for strategic industries are materially lower.

Gold has reached new all-time highs above $5,100 per ounce as investors rush to safe-haven assets amid the Middle East conflict and global market uncertainty, a significant boost for gold-mining countries like South Africa.

Natural gas prices are sharply higher after Iranian drone strikes forced Qatar (the world's largest LNG exporter) to declare force majeure and halt operations, cutting off about 20% of global liquefied natural gas supply.
moderate: WTI Crude at $90.90/barrel (+36% WoW) and Brent at $92.69 (+27%) reflect acute Strait of Hormuz disruption: ~140 million barrels of regional crude is stranded, OPEC+ announced a larger-than-expected production increase but barrels are largely inaccessible given the shipping halt; analysts warn Brent could exceed $100 if the conflict lasts beyond 4 weeks.

Gold at $5,158/oz continues its multi-year bull run, now compounded by the Iran conflict flight-to-safety bid; the metal benefits simultaneously from central bank buying (EM reserve diversification), USD weakness earlier in 2026, and an acute geopolitical risk premium; silver at $84.31 is tracking higher on both safe-haven and industrial demand.

Agricultural commodities are rising as the Middle East conflict disrupts shipping: wheat (+5.8% weekly) faces a dual shock: the Middle East is a large wheat importer and key shipping routes are disrupted; soybeans (+3.2%) are supported by China's continued import demand and Brazilian export strength; corn (+4.3%) reflects biofuel demand as energy prices spike globally.
expert: The WTI/Brent spread has narrowed to ~$1.79 (from a typical $3-5), reflecting the global nature of the supply shock and US SPR release speculation: with approximately 9mb/d off the market from facility damage and precautionary shutdowns, and OPEC+ production geographically constrained by Hormuz closure, the market's clearing mechanism is IEA strategic reserve coordination, a tool that buys weeks, not months, of price suppression.

Gold's rally above $5,100 represents a regime shift in the gold-real-rate relationship: previously gold tracked inversely to US real rates (TIPS yields); the current gold strength despite higher real rates (driven by CPI upside from energy) suggests the safe-haven bid is overriding the rate-discount mechanism, a pattern historically associated with tail-risk scenarios where the monetary policy reaction function itself becomes uncertain.

Agricultural commodity supercycle dynamics are being reinforced by the Iran shock: fertiliser (natural gas-intensive in production) prices are spiking with LNG, creating a second-order agricultural supply shock for the 2026/2027 growing season; the FAO food price index is likely to reverse its recent moderation; and the combination of energy and food price inflation in a single shock is historically the most damaging inflation configuration for EM sovereign credit.

commentary.beginner: Commodities are the raw materials that power the global economy - things like oil, gold, wheat, and copper. Their prices affect everything from the cost of filling your car to the price of bread. When oil rises, transport gets more expensive, which pushes up prices across the board. Gold often rises when people are worried about the economy.
commentary.moderate: Commodity markets are signalling mixed conditions. Energy prices remain subdued on soft China demand and resilient US shale supply, while gold continues to rally on central bank buying and safe-haven demand. Agricultural commodities are pressured by strong Southern Hemisphere harvests. The copper-to-gold ratio - a classic growth proxy - has been declining, consistent with a slowing global cycle.
commentary.expert: Cross-commodity signal extraction: the backwardation in crude (WTI M1-M6 spread ~$1.80) suggests physical tightness despite flat prices, consistent with OPEC+ compliance above 90%. Gold's move above $2,900 is driven less by real rates (still positive) and more by EM central bank reserve diversification (PBOC, RBI, NBP cumulative buying ~1,100t in 2024-25). Dr. Copper's sideways action reflects offsetting forces: China property drag vs. electrification pull. The GSCI/SPX ratio near 40-year lows signals extreme undervaluation of real assets vs. financial assets.
